speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to add a few words to the statement I made respecting the accident to the Burlington bridge.
A meeting was held in Ottawa today between the acting minister of highways for Ontario, the Hon. George Dunbar, and myself, and it was agreed that the first step in connection with the solution of the replacement of the Burlington canal bridge, which was wrecked by the steamer W. Fitzgerald on April 29, would be the replacement of the structure with a temporary non-movable bridge which would be started and carried to completion as early as possible.
Preceding this it will be necessary to remove the wrecked bridge, which work will be started immediately. It is expected that the removal of the wrecked bridge and the construction of the temporary bridge will be completed within the period of a month.
This is the first step in connection with what might be called the solution of the joint navigation and traffic problem.

The house resumed, from Monday, May 12, consideration of the motion of Mr. Fournier (Hull) for committee of supply.

When the house rose last night at eleven o'clock, Mr. Speaker, we were discussing the matter of floor prices under agricultural products, and dealing more particularly with the floor prices relating to animal products and their decline as a result of the outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease. I was discussing also what measures the government was taking with regard to that. I had pointed out that when this floor price legislation was introduced in 1944 the minister had made certain promises to the house and to the agricultural industry, concerning the basis on which those floor prices were to be established. I had gone on to point out that in my opinion, and I think in the opinion of the agriculture industry, these floor prices are too low, and that even these inadequate floor prices are not being paid the farmers, owing to the failure of the purchasers of farm products to co-operate fully with the government in maintaining them.
I should like to place certain figures on the record with respect to the adequacy or otherwise of these floor prices and whether or not they really cover the cost of production of agricultural products. Anyone who understands agriculture will agree that there are three or four main cost items entering into it. First, there is the cost of living of the farm family; second, the wages paid; third, the cost of farm machinery, and finally, farm taxes. I think probably those are the four main costs in connection with agricultural products.
With regard to farm living costs, I have in my hand the Canadian Statistical Review for April, 1952. At page 22 It indicates that in April, 1951, the index of farm living costs stood at 197-1. In January of 1952 it stood at 215-8, so in just a few months it had risen by 18-7 points. The cost of living index for
2150	HOUSE OF
Agricultural Products-Floor Prices Canadians as a whole has declined, but the index of farm living costs has not had a proportionate reduction.
With regard to farm wages, this morning I got in touch with the bureau of statistics, who were able to give me certain figures. These show that in 1940 the average wage paid on the farms of Canada was $41 per month, with board. By 1945 this had risen to $72, and by 1950 to $101. It has continued to rise, and I venture to say that at the present time it probably stands closer to $110. So in that period there has been a substantial rise in that item of cost to the farmer.
Then take farm taxes. Taxes on owned lands and buildings in Canada in 1939 amounted to $19,200,000. By 1945 these taxes had increased to $39,100,000 and by 1950 to $58,500,000. Again I am sure that if the figures were available for 1951 and 1952 they would show a further substantial increase.
As to operating costs on the farm, I asked the bureau what farmers spent in operating costs for tractors in that same period. I was astonished to find that in 1939 the operating cost of tractors was $22,800,000. By 1945 this had risen to $47,900,000, and by 1950 it had increased to $97 million. Of course more tractors are being used today than in 1939. But if we take farm machinery repairs, another large item of farm costs, we find that in 1939 the farmers of Canada paid $19,200,000 for farm machinery repairs. In 1945 they paid $31,100,000, and by 1950 these costs had risen to $58,500,000, or more than three times the cost in 1939.
Then take farm machinery itself. Using 1935-39 as a base of 100, we find that in 1939 the farm machinery index stood at 103-6. By 1945 it had risen to 115-1 and by 1950 to 186-8, and that increase is continuing. That is not the whole story, either. If you look over the prices of farm machinery you will find that the greater increases are in the prices of the newer types of machinery, the kind we are buying today. Those increases are greater than the increases in the prices of some of the older machines which enter into the cost index but are not being used as much today. For instance, in 1945 a ten or twelve-foot self-propelled combine cost about $2,800. Today the same combine costs just over $5,000, so it has almost doubled in cost in the last six years. That is why farmers are alarmed today. They see the prices of the things they have to sell going down while the cost of the things that enter into their cost of production continues to rise.


Just what has the drop amounted to in the prices of things the farmer has to sell? I am not going to give the figures on grain, though there has been a serious drop in price owing to the increase in the value of the Canadian dollar. There has been a drop of at least twenty cents in the price of wheat. Take animal products. In July of 1951 the index stood at 358-9. By February of this year it had dropped to 297-3, or a decline of 61-6 points in just a few months. And that was before or just at the time of the outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease in western Canada. Since that time there has been a further serious decline in the prices of agricultural products. It is no wonder that members of this house protest when they see that situation beginning to appear in Canada, with a serious decline in the purchasing power of the agriculture industry and no decline in their costs of production. That must inevitably result in less purchasing power for the farmers, and that reduced purchasing power sooner or later must result in unemployment in the industries in eastern Canada and elsewhere which supply the machinery industry for agriculture.
I hope hon. members from eastern Canada will not think that we in the west are simply making a plea for ourselves. We are not. We believe the best way to stop a decline or a depression in this country is to maintain a reasonable basis of prices for agricultural products, which will bear a fair relationship to the cost of what the farmer has to buy. That is the only way we can maintain a prosperous Canada. So I say every member in this house, whether from eastern Canada or western Canada, should be vitally interested in maintaining a reasonable floor price under agricultural products that will represent something near the cost of production. I must say that in my opinion the floor prices that have been established today do not nearly represent that cost.
Unless something is done by the government to see that these floor prices do represent the cost of production, and that when they do set a floor price it is payable to the producer, not to the processor of those products alone; that he shall have all the guarantee and that the industry itself shall be guaranteed only through the competition which the minister says must result from the present floor price-unless this is done, the farmers will not be satisfied. I do not think that competition has been sufficient to guarantee to the farmers the result which the minister I am sure desires. It certainly has not been enough; there has not been enough competition to maintain a reasonable floor price under eggs or under some of the other

agricultural products. Figures produced in this house and sent to the minister by individual farmers, by farm organizations, have I am sure proved that to him.
I think the government should take immediate steps to see that these floor prices, even though they are inadequate, are paid to the producers and not to the processors.

The question under discussion is the government's price support program and the failure of certain packing plants to pay the support price. With regard to the second point, I hope the minister will be in a position to assure us that conversations are now going on with the packing plants and that that difficulty will soon be eliminated.
It was on the other point I wanted to speak chiefly. Today is probably an opportune time to discuss the whole question of floor prices, because I think it is correct to say that this year is the first time that a real test has been made of the efficiency of operation of the government's floor price program.
I believe that to operate efficiently this program must have public opinion behind it. Moreover, I am satisfied that if the people of Canada realize the basis of the program they will be prepared to support it. Therefore I think it is unfortunate that at this time certain Canadian organizations should see fit to attack the government's support program. I have in mind the March news letter of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, printed in part in the Alberta wheat pool budget of March 28. I want to quote briefly from it, and from a short statement by the wheat pool in reply to it, and then make my own comments. It is under the heading: "Where do we stand?" and reads as follows:
Under the above heading, the March news letter of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce prints the following:
"Do we as Canadians believe in the principle of the free market, or do we not? Do we or do we not believe in a competitive economic system based on the law of supply and demand? These questions arise as the result of the action of the federal government in establishing a floor price for marketing of hogs-in fact pegging the price at the prevailing level.
"Here we have the rather anomalous situation of the Canadian people clamouring for a lower cost of living, and when the price of one of the primary factors entering into that cost of living-meat- starts to decline, the government steps in to make sure that prices won't go any lower. The completely astounding thing about this is the thunderous silence of Mr. and Mrs. Consumer.
No doubt the reason for that is that the general consumer and the public apparently have a far better understanding of the situation than the Canadian Chamber of Commerce have. I would just like to quote a
3, 1952
Agricultural Products-Floor Prices reply given in the wheat pool budget, which deals objectively with the question of free competitive enterprise:
It is easy to talk about free enterprise and the free market. But the same is more honoured in the breach than in the observance by Canadian business interests. In support of that statement we draw the attention of the chamber of commerce to the monopoly investigations into bakery establishments, flour milling, the making of dental and optical supplies, match manufacturing, etc., and those investigations, we believe, touched only the fringe. Those boys didn't practise free enterprise and abide by the free market!
Government assistance and government support of measures that have led to monopoly have been the rule ever since Canadian confederation.
I want to go on with the statement of the chamber of commerce:
The explanation which was given for the government's action, according to the press, was that if farmers took a heavy loss in hogs this year, they would not raise any next year. Then a shortage would develop and prices would again skyrocket. The other side of the situation of course was not mentioned at all. With a guaranteed price for hogs, producers will merrily continue to raise hogs beyond the desire or the capacity of the market.
The farmers of this country, Mr. Speaker, could, if they so decided, so adjust their operations as to increase prices under the law of supply and demand; that is to say, the farm organizations could organize and reduce agricultural production so that the prices would rise. Does the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, or anybody else, think for one minute that that would be to the advantage of the Canadian people? Would it be to the advantage of the other nations of the world? Would it be to the advantage of those nations which at the present time have many people on the verge of starvation? Surely a country like Canada, which is hoping to give a certain degree of leadership in the world, could not justify a reduction in production at this time. And yet the Canadian Chamber of Commerce criticize the government for supporting a program which helps to maintain production, and as a result they say it means higher prices. They apparently argue that it would be better to let the prices fall so that the production would be reduced.
I think we have an obligation to the world today to do everything possible that we can to maintain production at a high level, and I would suggest that one of the most logical ways to do that is to maintain a floor price under agricultural products. By that I do not mean an excessively high price; I mean a price that will bear a fair relationship to the prices of other commodities. I would say the program can be fully justified in many ways. First of all, let me give some background.
It will be recalled that in the depression years the prices of farm products fell very

Agricultural Products-Floor Prices much faster and very much farther than the prices of other commodities. While the prices of commodities of the secondary industries fell only 25 per cent, the prices of farm products fell over 65 per cent. And when time and again during the 1930's farmers and farm organizations would complain about the low level of agricultural prices they were told that nothing could be done about it because we were an exporting nation and therefore our prices internally had to be governed by the export prices. But it is interesting to note that that was not the policy of the secondary industries at that time. Many of those secondary industries maintained a two-price system. They sold at high prices in Canada, and then they sold at a lower price in the export market.
I recall that in the 1930's you could buy a Massey-Harris binder cheaper in Britain than you could buy it in Canada, so they were not maintaining their price on the export market; however, that was the policy at that time. True there were one or two minor exceptions, but generally speaking the prices of agricultural products were maintained at the prices that obtained in the export market. When the war came on and prices rose we adopted a price control policy in this country and price ceilings were placed upon agricultural products. The farmers then found themselves in this somewhat difficult position. During the ten years of the depression they had had to accept world market prices, prices that were far below cost of production, and many farmers went heavily into debt; many of them went bankrupt. Well, if an industry has to accept world prices when prices are low, surely it is justified in expecting to get world market prices when they rise, because that is the only way they can make up the losses they suffer during the time they are selling at prices which are far below the cost of production.
The government apparently realized that and said to the farmers: We are going to maintain a price ceiling on your products, but that is part of a general stabilization program. In return for that we are going to see to it that in the future the prices of your commodities are not allowed to fall below a fair level. And so the Agricultural Prices Support Act was put into operation. We commended the government when that legislation was brought down. I thought it good legislation then, and I think it is good legislation today. Certain changes need to be made, but the general principle behind the Agricultural Prices Support Act in my opinion is absolutely sound. When that act was put into operation, for the first few years it was not necessary to use it because prices were high. However

in 1950 the prices of certain commodities began to fall out of line. Agricultural organizations took a great deal of interest in the manner in which the act was to be used to ascertain what the support prices should be.
At the convention of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture held at Niagara the minister dealt in a general way with the basis of the formula, and stated that prices for farm produce would be maintained at a level which would afford the same relationship to the prices of other commodities as existed from 1943 to 1945 at the time the Agricultural Prices Support Act was put into operation.
The interesting point today is to compare the prices of farm products on the basis of that formula. With that in mind I wrote to the bureau of statistics asking them to give me what prices of farm products should be today on the basis of that formula, so that the prices of farm products today would bear its same relationship to the prices of other commodities as existed in 1943-45.
According to the figures they have given me, in some cases the floor is a little higher; but in most cases it is lower than it should have been. This table is prepared under four columns, and I should like to place it on Hansard. Before doing so however I shall read the items because, as I go along, I shall comment upon them.
The first item concerning which I asked information was wheat No. 1 northern, per bushel, delivered at Fort William, Port Arthur or Vancouver. I realize that wheat does not come under the Agricultural Prices Support Act, but I asked for those figures only to find out what the price of wheat would be if it had been under the act. It is interesting to note that the average price for 1943-45 for No. 1 northern wheat, basis Fort William, was $1,391. In column 2, which relates to the general wholesale index today, the price would be $2,306. On the other hand, if we compare that price with the price that farmers have to pay for other commodities today the price of wheat would then be $2,530. The actual price for wheat today is about $1.80, under the international wheat agreement. So actually the price the farmer is receiving today under the international wheat agreement is 70 cents less than the price he should receive under the formula of the Agricultural Prices Support Act.
The next item about which I asked was hogs, grade B-l, dressed, Winnipeg, per hundredweight. The actual average price in 1943-45 was $16,341. Column 2, in relation to the wholesale price index today, shows a price of $27,093. Under column 3, which

shows the relationship to prices that farmers have to pay for other commodities, the price would be $29,724. The actual price at the time of this report-January, 1952-was $25,390. So that the farmers were receiving around $4 less than the support price should be under the formula of the Agricultural Prices Support Act. I believe the floor price is somewhere in the neighbourhood of $25; therefore the price I have indicated here is about $3.50 per hundredweight under the formula.
The next item refers to good steers, up to 1,050 pounds, Winnipeg, per hundredweight. The average price in 1943-45 was $11,265. The price under the general wholesale index would be $18,677, and as related to the prices the farmers pay for other commodities it would be $20,491. The price at the time the report was issued in January was $30,670. The support price now is about $23.35, so that the support price is actually about $2.85 above the formula.
With regard to eggs, grade A large, at Winnipeg, the actual average price 1943-45 was $[DOT]404; the figure in column 2 is $-670, and in column 3 $-735. The price in January of this year was $-405. So the price of eggs at that time was about 33 cents a dozen less than it should have been under the Agricultural Prices Support Act formula. However I understand that the price of eggs today in many parts of western Canada is far below 40 cents. Indeed, I heard one member mention 10 cents a dozen. But even if 40 cents was being paid, that would be 30 cents less than it should be under the formula.
The next item is Cheddar cheese No. 1 white, per pound, f.o.b. Montreal warehouse. The actual average price in 1943-45 was $-205; the figure in column 2 is $ [DOT] 340 and in column 3 $-373, with the January price at $-440. So the price of cheese at that time was above the price to be paid under the formula-approximately 7 cents above that price.
Then we come to creamery butter, per pound at Winnipeg, and we find that the average price for 1943-45 was $-352. The figure in column 2 is $-587 and in column 3 $*640. The January price in this year was $[DOT]670. So that that price is slightly above the formula.

My only suggestion is that you should address your questions to the agricultural prices support board, because they are the people who can give you the information based upon any statement that I made.

I can quite understand that the agricultural prices support board could give me the basis it is working on, but I want statistics to show what the support prices would be on the basis of the formula the minister outlined to the Canadian Federation of Agriculture and this house.

There has been some criticism of the formula. Many organizations feel that 194345 is not an entirely satisfactory base period. I agree, but on the other hand I would say that the formula is a whole lot better than nothing at all. We wanted a formula and the minister has given us one. With the help of the bureau of statistics we have been able to work out what the support prices should be on the basis of that formula. It is shown quite clearly that in the majority of cases the prices of other commodities have risen faster than the prices of farm products.
In the past most farm organizations have advocated that the floor prices for agricultural products should provide a parity income so that the income of the farmer will bear the same relationship to the national income as farm population does to the national population. If that formula was adopted, the prices of farm products would be considerably higher than is provided for in this formula, because today the farm population is about 25 per cent of the total population, whereas the farmers' share of the national income-I have not the latest figures-I believe is somewhere around 10 or 12 per cent.
It is 9-9 per cent.

I am informed by the hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Fair), who obtained the figure from the bureau of statistics, that it is 9-9 per cent. There you

have the farmers who represent 25 per cent of the population receiving only 9 [DOT] 9 per cent of the national income. That shows quite clearly that they are not receiving what could be called a parity price based on income. But I am glad, as I have said, that the government has brought in the Agricultural Prices Support Act, even though it is based upon a formula that seems to provide prices not sufficiently high. Again I say that that is far better than no support prices at all.
It seems to me that the important point is that the packing companies in Canada should be made to live up to the support prices. If they continue the practice of paying less than the support prices it will only destroy the efficiency of the operation of the whole program.
I have referred to the fact that the one way in which farmers can overcome a loss through the operations of the law of supply and demand would be to restrict production. On the other hand, even without the formula or without the Agricultural Prices Support Act the prices of agricultural products probably could be maintained fairly high if the government had an international policy which made it possible to move our surpluses to those nations that need them. I will not say that the Agricultural Prices Support Act would not be needed, but it would not be necessary to use it to anything like the extent it has

had to be used when there was no means of exporting our surplus production.
I was interested in the speech made by the Minister of Agriculture before the food and agriculture organization when he stated that unless some better method of marketing was found he could hardly expect the farmers of Canada to expand their production. There is no use in the farmers expanding their production unless there is a market. Unfortunately as yet the FAO has not been able to submit any proposals for moving farm surpluses that meet with agreement by the member nations. They brought down a proposal for a world food board, but that was rejected. They brought down a proposal for an international commodity clearing house, but that was rejected. At the present time each nation has to depend upon its own resources to market its farm products.
I want to commend the government upon the agreement they have made with Great Britain and New Zealand for the disposal of beef. While there is a loss involved, it is far better to suffer a loss than to have beef rotting on the market or to have the farmers doing everything they can to reduce the production of cattle. It is a temporary expedient, but it is one which I think is justified. I hope if the government has any difficulty in disposing of surpluses in the future they will not hesitate to tread new paths. I do not believe that the use of the old orthodox channels of trade will provide the means for moving our surpluses of food products to the nations which need them. Ways and means of moving our surpluses to the nations facing widespread starvation must be found. If the practice of reducing the production of food, whilst millions of people are on the verge of starvation, becomes prevalent it will create fertile ground for the spread of communism throughout the world.

Mr. Speaker, I want to take a few minutes to enter this discussion on price spreads. Throughout the war years and some of the years following, the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) and the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) repeatedly asked the producers of this nation to keep up and expand their production of foodstuffs. They were told that ceilings would be placed on their products and that floors would be provided for in later years when markets might be declining. I think the institution of support prices was just and proper.
A number of the floor prices now prevailing are not satisfactory to the producers. As has been indicated, their cost of production is still rising. The bureau of statistics point out that the prices of farm machinery of the 55704-136J
Agricultural Products-Floor Prices newer type will be advanced during the current year over the previous year. Farm wages and other costs are still increasing, despite the fact that they are already at an all-time high.
A question was asked today about placing a floor under cheese. This is a matter which affects the farmers of eastern Canada more than those of western Canada. I have talked to a number of dairy people during the past days and weeks and I found them in a rather sorry plight, I think through no fault of their own. They deserve some assistance by way of floor prices.
What I want to refer to chiefly at the moment is the floor prices under beef and hogs. The floor price under hogs was announced some time ago at a figure somewhat lower than that which had been asked for by organized agriculture. Taking into account the cost of feed, labour and all that, I do not think the price is sufficiently high.
With respect to the beef price, it is true that the government is working under rather vexing circumstances. These floor prices were announced early in the month of April, and throughout much of the country they are certainly not working satisfactorily. In the Winnipeg Tribune of May 8, the following report appeared:
With no dominion price supports Alberta processors are getting cattle at bargain counter prices and hardly making an impression on available supplies.
Alberta beef, laid down in Winnipeg at 39 cents a pound, carcass weight, is being sold for the same basic 92 cents a pound retail as Manitoba beef sides from city processors at 46 cents a pound.
The article goes on to point out the difficulty of contending with that sort of thing, and also that the consumers are not getting any benefit at this time. I asked a question of the Minister of Agriculture about these prices and what guarantee there was that they would go through to the producer. I understand that because of provincial embargoes great difficulty is being encountered. I am amazed that the Department of Justice has not given some ruling as to whether these provincial embargoes are justified. It shows lack of decision on the part of the Department of Justice, and certainly it is very bad for the country that the various provinces should balkanize the nation as they have been doing for many weeks.
Like the previous speaker (Mr. Quelch) I want to commend the minister and his staff for the efforts they have made in arranging the * agreement between New Zealand, Great Britain and Canada with respect to beef. However, the agreement will far from take care of the surplus beef in Canada. I have

Agricultural Products-Floor Prices not the exact figures before me, but I think I am safe in saying it will not take care of twenty per cent of the beef that we exported last year to the splendid United States market. Therefore hon. members will readily realize what a tremendous surplus of beef we shall have on our hands after the fulfilment of the contract for the current year between Canada, New Zealand and Great Britain. As time goes on I hope we shall be able to increase the amount of beef handled under this arrangement.
Then again, the price floors are on a monthly basis. I believe that they are to run until the first of July, and that there will then be a new adjustment. It is almost impossible for cattle breeders or producers to plan their operations on such a basis. I am fearful also as to what may happen to many producers this fall. As far back as I can remember, we have always had a great run of cattle during the fall months. People put cattle on grass and then cannot take care of them through the winter. I assume that many producers will try to carry more cattle through the winter, but many of them will be unable to do so. Some plan will have to be worked out to take care of the marketing of surplus beef during the fall months.
I have never yet heard a statement in the house as to the details of the working out of the floor price on beef and how it is carried through the various grades so as to ensure that the producer will be guaranteed the floor price. I should like to see such a statement put on Hansard. When the outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease was announced in the third week of February the prices for cattle prevailing in the Winnipeg stockyards on February 22 were as follows: Steers, 30 cents; heifers, 28 cents; cows 21 cents; bulls, 23 cents; stock and feeder steers, 27 cents; stock and feeder heifers, 25 cents; cows, 20 cents, and veal calves 30 cents. Some months previously the market had been considerably higher. Therefore when one compares these figures with the present floor prices or the prices prevailing, one will see there is a very great difference.
While a great many producers are trying to help in this difficult time by holding back their livestock, some large producers of both hogs and cattle have stated that they are now going to get rid of their breeding stock and take their loss as at this time. It is a very confusing situation. I hope that the government will reconsider the question of floor prices and do more than they have done to stabilize production and assist producers. It means a great deal to the entire economy of

Canada, apart from the producers themselves, and at the present time it is a very unsatisfactory state of affairs.
Mr. Speaker-

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Gardiner (Minister of Agriculture):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker-
I hope the minister is not closing the debate.
No, I did not start it. The debate is on an amendment moved from the other side of the house.
There is no amendment.
There is an amendment to the motion to go into supply.
No.
It does not matter. It is not my motion and I have not spoken so far.
Are you going to move an amendment?

No, I am not going to move an amendment.
The discussion last night and this afternoon has been on the question of floor prices. I am quite aware of the fact that one can take any set of prices, discuss them back and forth and arrive at all kinds of conclusions, but there are a few facts that I think are selfevident and that have a bearing upon the question. The first one is that in 1943 and 1944 we had the highest production that we have ever had. Those two years were the highest production years in agriculture. Production is not nearly so high now in some lines. It is just as high in wheat, but it is not as high in livestock products as it was in 1943 and 1944. Nevertheless, in spite of all that has been said this afternoon and last night, and whether or not floor prices had anything to do with it, we got twice as much in money for our farm products last year as we did in those years. I know that the first argument that is put forward after that statement is made is: Oh yes, but the costs of everything are higher now than they were then. However, before we would be in nearly as bad a position as has been outlined by some hon. members everything would have to cost at least twice as much in order that there might even be an argument about it at all.
Obviously, from statistics prepared by the same bureau that prepared these other statistics, we got $2,800 million for our farm products last year and $1,400 million in the years to which reference has been made. That is just double, and if anyone is trying to reason that the farmer is worse off because he has got double I would not agree with him.
That would be in dollars.

That is in dollars. I say you can take all the considerations and argue yourself into any kind of decision you like if you want to start to argue from that point of view. It is like a person saying that because you load meat on the boat in Australia at 12 cents and it costs you 48 cents in Canada to do the same, you can start from there and say that Australia is four times as badly off. As a matter of fact there are so many factors entering into an argument of that kind that one would get lost before he could get half way through it. You certainly could not finish it in a forty minute speech. The obvious fact is that last year we got twice as much for what we sold as we did in the years that are taken as the basis for the relationship between our prices then and prices now.
In addition, we did not produce as much last year as we did in those years. That has some bearing upon the argument that our friends of the chamber of commerce are using, to the effect that you can affect your prices by producing less or more. If you produce too much then you will probably reduce your prices.	If you produce
too little you will probably raise your prices.	I do not	think that the
farmers have been unwise in what they have done. I have heard members get up and criticize the government because farmers have reduced their production of certain products. As a matter of fact in most of these matters the farmers do not pay any attention to the government at all. They run their own show; they run their own business, and they know more about it than most members of the House of Commons. They realized that if they produced fifty per cent more hogs this year than they did previously, they would not get as much money for the greater number as they did for what they produced before. They realized that, and they carried on their activities accordingly. The farmers are producing those things which they think will help them to get along best, and the very fact that they got twice as much money last year producing less of the product than in the years referred to is an indication that they know what they are doing.
On the question of floor prices, it has been suggested time after time that we have a fund of $200 million and have not used very much of it. That carries me back to the debates of eight years ago, in 1944, when we introduced the bill under which we have the fund of $200 million to use in encouraging farmers to do one thing or another and to
Agricultural Products-Floor Prices give them a better return for their products. The fact is, as I said the other day, that is a revolving fund. There is $200 million set up, and when we were discussing it eight years ago some members proposed that we ought to put a limit of four years on the operation of the Agricultural Prices Support Act. I took the position in the house at that time that it was eighteen years after the end of the first war before we came to the end of the period during which the difficulties had been experienced which we might find it necessary to look after now. It is now eight years after the passing of that act, and I think it can be truly said that the reasons we were anticipating eight years ago that would necessitate the passing of this legislation have never yet happened.
The reasons that were in our minds at that time were that we were going to have a great slump in prices in this country, particularly a great slump in agricultural prices. We had good reason for fearing that. The argument read a few moments ago by the member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch) is the old argument that we have heard from those who are representing a group who passed that resolution. It is the same argument that has prevailed for centuries, if you like-certainly before the beginning of the lifetime of any member of this house- when it was argued that the way to stop inflation is to force down the farmer's prices first. You can force his prices down by denying him credits; denying him this and that; denying him money to spend on things. You can force down prices there, and by forcing down prices there you can control inflation.
The one undertaking the government gave, if they gave any at all, was to try to prevent that kind of thing happening at the end of this war. It has happened at the end of every other war, but it has not yet happened at the end of this one. I am not going to claim that is only because of the floor price legislation of this government. It has not happened at the end of this war because the people in other countries, as well as this, have been following a policy which has not resulted in that coming about in the manner in which it did before. Nevertheless, the remarks made by the member for Souris (Mr. Ross) and the member for Acadia are correct in this, that they have commended the government for having set a floor price policy and for having put it into effect. We have not used up the $200 million. I have said on a number of occasions, and I repeat it now, that if we had used up the $200 million the first year or the second year doing things that it was not necessary for us

Agricultural Products-Floor Prices an animal that had foot-and-mouth disease. So no one wants to eat any of those animals coming from Saskatchewan.
Fortunately we have had experiences of this kind before. In 1937 we went out to Saskatchewan and Alberta and bought 93,000 head of cattle, which we put in pastures. The government built the fences; we had no community pastures then, as we have now. These cattle were pastured down at Carberry, Manitoba, for the summer, and then we auctioned them off to feeders all over Canada. We sold them for higher prices than they could have been sold for by any other method, but for very low prices as we consider prices today. That cost the government $300,000. In those days it was questioned whether a government should spend $300,000 to help the livestock producers in western Canada; but the job was done.
In doing that job we acquired experience which stands us in good stead now. We can go back to Saskatchewan today and take care of the situation existing there. As I said last night, my assistant is going out again tomorrow, and Mr. Shaw is going with him. We have already made contacts with the wheat pool and others, and we think we can set up an organization that can deal with the situation. But they cannot handle it by putting the meat under the contracts we have been able to make, nor can they handle it by getting a decision on the question of whether the provinces were acting illegally when they imposed the restrictions they have imposed. In my own heart I have a feeling that the provinces are within their rights when they try to stop disease from spreading from one area to another. And I have a feeling that whether they are right or wrong they are going to do it anyway. If they cannot do it by law, they will do it in some other way. No people anywhere are going to allow you to deliberately ship cattle with foot-and-mouth disease, or hogs that may be subject to it, out of one area into another and particularly from one province to another. If that is what we are dealing with, then I have some doubts as to whether the provinces are within their rights or not. It has been said that the Department of Justice should have given a decision long ago. Well, the Department of Justice has given the same kind of decision on this as it gives on anything else. The Department of Justice naturally says: "Well, the courts are there; try it out." We might get some fellow up in Saskatoon to ship a carload of cattle down to Winnipeg and run them across the boundary line. Whether the railways would take them across or not I do not know. Probably they would not take them, but even

if we could get a drover to load them on a truck and then down to Winnipeg, and the shipper got himself arrested-well, if he did that, it would take him about four months to find out whether he was right or not, and in the meantime probably he would be in jail. You could settle it that way, and Justice will tell you and anyone else will tell you that. You can have a test, because you can take it to the courts, and it will take anywhere from two or three months to six months to get it settled.
That is not good enough for this job. We have to settle this thing in a few days, in a few weeks at the outside. Therefore, when Manitoba says: "We will not kill any Saskatchewan cattle", I do not think they have any legal right to say that. But when this house put through the legislation a year ago to provide for emergencies, it gave authority to declare an emergency only if it had something to do with defence. So far as I have been able to search out, this has nothing to do with defence. Perhaps if you took a long enough view of it it has; I do not know. But in any case there is no way that we can prove at the present time that this is an emergency and say to Manitoba: "You have got to kill the beef." If I could declare an emergency it would take six months to find out as to whether we are right or wrong. In the meantime we could go on killing beef. We are not able to do that because there is no defence emergency. We know that from the Department of Justice, and there is only one other thing to do, and that is for us to try to persuade Manitoba to remove their embargo. We finally arrived at an agreement with British Columbia. We have an agreement with Alberta. I do not think our discussion was ever out in the open. Our discussions were always with them where they should be on a thing like this, more or less behind closed doors. We had plenty of trouble in our discussions in arriving at conclusions as to what we were going to do, but we eventually got there and without any hangover, and now the stock is moving out of Alberta. But there has never been a change in Manitoba since the day that it was determined that they would let sheep and pigs in but they would not let cattle in.
I cannot understand the reasoning in connection with it, but nevertheless the reasoning is there. Now, with the possibilities of moving beef out of Alberta and pork out of Alberta under the British arrangement and moving beef out of Ontario and hogs out of Ontario, there is not much to worry about anywhere else for the time being, excepting Saskatchewan. Most people do not realize

that there are more cattle marketed out of Saskatchewan than out of Alberta in normal times. There are more cattle there to be marketed now than can be marketed. But they have no big packing houses to take them as they have in Alberta. They have large packing houses in Edmonton; they have large packing houses in Calgary and smaller ones in Lethbridge and so on. But we have just some dinky little packing houses in Prince Albert, Saskatoon and Regina, and then one with a little larger capacity in Moose Jaw. But they could not begin to handle the livestock that are produced in Saskatchewan, and they have never had to. We have depended on Winnipeg, and we still depend on Winnipeg. Until they let our cattle into Winnipeg, they cannot be slaughtered to be shipped anywhere else in great quantity. That is our great problem yet. It is there.
I am not sure what Manitoba is going to do-I think I know what they are going to do. I think I know what they will do inside a very short time, but I think they will do it much quicker if they are left alone until they are good and ready than if we take court action against them and try to force them and wait until the court decides. I think we can do it the other way more quickly. I say that for this reason. With all these difficulties going on I would like to ask hon. members just how they think we could have enforced floor prices. Were we going to tell this fellow that he has got to pay for animals when he has no slaughter house to kill them in? Are we going to tell the other fellow that he has got to take the farmer's cattle, whether he has grass or not, and pay the price? We had to create a situation under which this surplus could be moved, and it could only be moved by reaching an agreement similar to the one we have reached, or doing something else about it because we could not reach an agreement. But fortunately we did reach it and things are moving now, and I think the floor prices are being established.
The organization, as I said a moment ago, that we will probably put in will be an organization similar to that of 1937. With the wheat pool organized as it is now to deal in livestock as well as in wheat, we may be able to make some arrangement under which they can do for us what we had to do for ourselves before. But whether they do it or not, an organization will be put in there to do something similar to what was done in Alberta by the Alberta government. They have auctions that are held here and there all over the province. They have had them organized for years, and those auctions have been held this year. The farmers have brought 55704-137
Agricultural Products-Floor Prices in the cattle they have and have sold them to other farmers, and the farmers have taken them home and are feeding them.
In Saskatchewan, on the other hand, we have a million and a half acres of land in government pastures, and we have room on those pastures for something like 10,000 to
20,000	head of cattle. We have not the slaughter houses to kill them. We could not get the meat on the market in the next two or three weeks, or maybe a month, even if we did have slaughter houses to kill them. If farmers need cash and must have it we will say to them: "All right, bring your cattle in to some particular point and we shall have somebody there to auction them for you. We shall have somebody there to pay you if we buy them", and those that are fit for slaughter we will send for slaughter. Those that can go in to the pastures we can send to our pastures.
We believe we will get through on an arrangement of that kind without any loss to the government, and that we will be of some service to those who are there and who are dependent on the sale of livestock in the next few weeks or months in order to get along until harvest time when they can get some money out of their grain. But we will be saying to others: Keep all the cattle home on your farms that you can. Sell all those, which you must sell, to your neighbours if possible. Don't come near us at all unless you have to. But if you must come to us in order to get rid of some of them, well, then, take them to this point and that point, which will be indicated, and there will be a proper set-up there, handled either by the wheat pool or by ourselves, in order to take care of the situation.
Under that method I think we will be able to maintain the floor price; but it will not be because we have a law which says to the packers or anybody else: "You must pay it". It will be because we are prepared to pay ourselves, and handle the situation. And simply because we are prepared to pay, if anyone else wishes to stay in business he will have to pay. That is the only basis on which we can operate.
I would say to the members of the C.C.F. party that if they want to do it in any other way, the only other government body in the province of Saskatchewan that has anything to do with Saskatchewan, other than this one, is the C.C.F. government. They have the authority to do it if they want to do it. They could do it-even a good Ontario Conservative government has proven that during the last year. They took over cheese at a price. They set the price for cheese; they enforced the price for cheese. It was not

Agricultural Products-Floor Prices this government that did it, and any provincial government can do it but no federal government can.
There is only one thing that might bother them, namely: what are they going to do with the surplus? Ontario had no trouble with cheese last year because Britain took it. But this year, when Britain was not ready to take it, they had some difficulty. But there is no other province in Canada that produces a surplus of cheese. And why they have any difficulty, I do not know. They can set their price; they can set the whole method of handling, if they wish to. They can say what the price will be, and they can enforce it. But this government cannot do that. And so all this talk which shouts "when you put a floor price on, why do you not enforce it?" is answered by the fact that we have not the authority. It rests with the province. We can only offer to buy and unless we wish to drive all others out of business the price must not be an incentive price. In other words, if it were a price to induce greater production we would drive all others out of business.
We put on a floor price which says to the people who produce the product, "If you cannot sell it to anyone else for more, we will take it at this price. We do not want it, but we will take it at this price, and we will carry it along." Then, occasionally we add this: "If we do make money we will pay it to you in the form of a participation payment, an interim payment or a final payment." We usually like to say that. Because, after all, we do not want to make money on the handling of farmers' products. We want the money to go back to them.
Then, on this question, "Why do you not see that when we set a floor price the packer pays the price to the farmer?", I say that the floor prices that we set, and the only floor prices we can set, are for buying direct from the farmer. If we go out to Saskatchewan and buy live cattle and put them in a pasture, we will have men sitting at a table right alongside the auction lot handing the man his cheque as he walks away. In other words, he will know he gets the money. When we buy butter from farmers, or from factories belonging to farmers, at so much a pound-58 cents a pound-well, they are paid for it. And, on the other hand, if a packing house buys it at 58J cents and prevents our getting it, then they pay for it, and we do not pay for it. The farmer gets the money direct from the packing house.
Are you not buying eggs and butter and other products from the packers?
We do not buy from the packers.
You have to take it from the packers at a certain price.

No, when we buy any farm product, whether it is cheese or butter or meat or anything else, we use the packing house as a facility through which to pass the product. And we may use the staff of some of the packers in order to handle the product through their plants, on to the boats, to be shipped to Great Britain. But they are only the facility which we authorize to do our job for us. We to all intents and purposes buy the product right from the producer or from his agent.
Is that the case with eggs? Is that so when you take delivery of eggs at a set price in September?

With eggs it would be the case, if we had ever bought any. But the plan with eggs is different from all the other plans; and the house understood it was different at the time. We said to the dealers in eggs, right across Canada, "If you have any eggs left in storage on the first of October, from the first of October to the end of the year, we are prepared to take those eggs off your hands at 38 cents, plus carrying charges." Someone said last night that carrying charges were five cents. Well, I think in most cases carrying charges amount to four cents. With eggs at 38 cents, we undertake to take them at 42 cents, adding on the four cents. We say we are prepared to take them at 42 cents from anyone who will turn them over to us. We have been operating for three years, and have not bought an egg.
Is it not the same in connection with pork, that you offered to purchase so many millions of pounds of canned pork from the packers at a fixed price?

No, that is not so. And it
is not exactly the same as we first intended it to be.
But you have offered that for it?

But we have taken over some pork at different times. Under the egg proposal, however, we have not taken over any eggs.
A while ago I was satisfied, from the information I was getting, that there were people who were not paying the floor price. As soon as we were satisfied of that we notified all those people that they need not come to us after the first of October asking us to take over the surplus of eggs. I understand that kind of thing stopped right there. I may say that some hon. members are to

be congratulated upon having been among the first to bring the matter to my attention. But I do think that if it is stopped it ought to be admitted that the system is functioning. It seems to me that we set up a set of principles, and every time any little thing goes wrong in connection with them, you become the chief grousers. And that is the quickest way to kill it.
If people have a system, if people try to establish fair prices and try to stand up against what has been criticized in the handling of products in an extreme form of private dealings, and that set-up runs into a little trouble, the only way you are going to perpetuate that kind of thing is to stop shouting about the little mistakes made here and there along the line.
I do not know whether we have got the right way of handling eggs or not. But I do know we tried it as an experiment in the first year. I do know that in the second year everybody interested came back and said, "Do it that way over again"-because there was not a single thing to complain about. When we handled it the second year everyone said the same thing. The only criticism that was made in the second year was, "You ought to put the price a little higher."
Then we went back into it on the same basis, in the third year. Now we are in the midst of the third year, and some people tell us they have found that some things have slipped. Well, all I wish to say about it is that you cannot get out of it so easily just by saying that it is the packers. After all, there are a lot of eggs that never go near the packing houses. There has been talk about this 10 cents and 15 cents; but to my knowledge a packing house has never had any dealings in those areas. Where the packing house has been the price has been 28 cents or 29 cents.
I might agree that it is still a little low. I think when they get down to 32 cents that is about as low as they ought to get. When they have been down to 29, and in other places to 28, there has been the heavy freight rate to consider, for shipping long distances.
But, after all, I think I am correct in saying that, with very few exceptions, the floor price has been maintained. I am willing to admit that one of the places where the price has been low has been down in the constituency of the hon. member for Assini-boia (Mr. Argue). That is one of the places. And I think he will agree that that is just about as far away from a packing house as one could get. And it was not really the packing house that caused most of the trouble there; and the same applies to other areas.

The information I have is with respect to the prices paid to farm women on eggs shipped to creameries. That is their ordinary place of marketing.
All the creameries I know of in that part of Saskatchewan are owned by farmers.
Not all.
Well, they all are down in that section of the country.
Oh, no.

And as a matter of fact those situations should be dealt with on their merits. As a matter of fact, I find that people who are organized into companies, no matter how they are organized, are human beings. Sometimes they go in one direction a little too long, and have to be turned back, even when they are co-operatives. So that if that was true in that section of the country it could only be true in one way, and that is through the co-operative creameries in not handling them as they should have-because that is what they all are. That is what they are.
Not all of them.

That is all they would pay. If they paid more there would be that much competition for anyone else who wanted to buy. If the co-operatives which are there paid twenty cents nobody would get them for ten. That is the situation that exists there.
I think that is all I wish to say. Under the circumstances I think this is going along fairly well. No one anticipated the troubles we have had because of disease coming into the country. It is being handled as best it can. I think it is pretty well agreed that the job is being fairly well done. If we do not get it moving smoothly quite as quickly as some people would like, it is not because we have no wish or desire to do so, it is simply because we could not get things moving fast enough in some things over which we did not have absolute control.

Just a question in relation to the minister's announcement of the government's program for the buying of live cattle. Is it the intention of the government to buy only good or choice steers, or is it the intention to buy various grades of cattle?

It is our intention to try to persuade the farmer to keep at home anything which he will probably be able to market if and when the United States market opens. In the first place, we are going to try to persuade him to keep everything home that he can keep home, everything that he feels he can feed for a number of months

Agricultural Products-Floor Prices ahead. Whether those are good steers or whether they are canners, we are not going to send anyone who must sell home with his stock.
If they bring them into market we will try to persuade some other farmer to buy them and take them home. We will hold an auction and allow him to bid against us and everybody else. If a farmer is prepared to pay a little more than the floor price, we will welcome that fact because we would not need to have anything more to do with those particular cattle. If some packing house is prepared to pay more than the floor price we will say to them, "take them away." But if we are not able to get rid of some we will have them taken to our pastures. That is stating in a few words the plan as it is in my mind, but I do not know that it is in anybody else's up to now.
Not passed by the government?
The order in council authorizes us to buy cattle or beef at the floor price.

Mr. Speaker, anyone who is in the predicament which I now face will agree that the life of a member of parliament is far from being rosy. During the last three week ends I have visited my constituency when many representations have been made to me. I was rash enough to promise that on the first occasion that presented itself I would speak on floor prices on agricultural products. I made that promise as late as yesterday at noon and it happens that the day I came back the house was discussing that very question. Without having sufficient time at my disposal to get all the information I would have liked to get, I feel I must keep my promise and rise to speak at this moment.
Anyone who speaks on agricultural matters following the minister is at a disadvantage. My own experience being what it is, I feel that my position is worse than that of others who have taken part or who might take part in this debate. Before proceeding I should like to congratulate the minister upon the deal that has been arranged between Great Britain, the United States and New Zealand. I wish also to congratulate him upon the masterful speech he made this afternoon to which considerable publicity should be given. I am sure it will answer many of the questions people have in their minds on this matter.
Everybody knows that I am no expert on agriculture, that I have no practical experience in agriculture. I do not even pretend to have any theoretical experience or knowledge. My remarks are based on the

representations which have been made to me by agricultural societies and private individuals in my constituency.
The main question facing those in Quebec who go in for mixed farming on a small scale is the cost of raising hogs and the small margin of profit that is left to them under the present floor. The majority of these farmers contend that there is not even a margin of profit, that they cannot produce at the floor price of 26 cents f.o.b. Toronto which has been fixed by the government. I admit that a few of them who seem to be better organized and have had more experience say that they can produce at 24 cents, but they admit that they are in the minority.
Their main obstacle is the cost of feed. When the feed is moved to Quebec or the eastern parts of Canada the margin of profit to the farmer is considerably reduced. These people contend that if the price of hogs is to remain at the present level for any period of time further relief should be given by way of a larger subsidy than the 30 cents per hundredweight now provided by the government on the transportation of feed to Quebec or eastern Canada.
As I say, I have no personal experience in this matter but bona fide farmers tell me that they have no objection to the price being fixed at 26 cents as long as they are able to make a reasonable margin of profit. Most of them feel that the present system is better than the one that prevailed after the first war when there was no floor at all. They admit that the government has adopted a wise policy by coming to an agreement with the packers, but this does not have the same effect in eastern Canada as it has in other parts of the country. However, whatever difficulty we had for a short time in Quebec has been eliminated through the activities of the minister's department.
It is hoped that the present agreement with Great Britain will facilitate matters as far as we are concerned. As far as the agreement with the packers is concerned, our farmers find the basis is sound but at the moment all cold storage space has been taken up and since there are no canning facilities available in Quebec the situation there became acute. The government agreed to accept all canned pork under the agreement but since the Quebec slaughtering houses are not equipped for canning it became impossible for them to support the market at the agreed prices.
There was one co-operative in Montreal and one in Quebec but neither has any facilities for canning. Then there was a private enterprise built by an individual who was a great

help to the farmers for some time. He made money during the period when we were shipping to Great Britain. He continued to supply the British market long after other packing houses had gone back to the domestic trade. The farmers at that time were, I am told, well satisfied with the treatment they received from him.
Afterward he made arrangements to supply the United States market and our people were able to ship their hogs to him at lower costs of transport and yet be paid on the basis of Montreal as far as general prices were concerned. But when this agreement was made with the packers it was found that all cold storage facilities were filled and no canning facilities were available in Quebec. The companies manufacturing canning equipment told these people that it would take from eight months to a full year before they could supply any of this equipment. This company therefore stopped maintaining the prices but now has corrected the situation. Therefore the only reproach made by the farmers at that time was because they were not notified on the day that company stopped supporting the market. At one period our farmers were a bit worried because they were getting substantially lower prices, a top of 20 cents instead of 26 cents, but due to the interference of the minister this company has now sent cheques to all those who had sold to it at lower prices, and the situation is now remedied as far as that is concerned. However, this same packing house, which formerly slaughtered about
8,000	a week, is now taking about 1,200 at the most, and the people of our district have to ship to the Montreal market. The 26 cents applies to Montreal so there is only 23J or 24 cents available to them for grade A. They are not on the basis they hoped to be when they first considered the statement of the minister, but the statement said f.o.b. Toronto or Montreal so there was no misrepresentation.
The fact that the local slaughtering house supported the market for a short period until the cold storage was full led them to believe the price applied to all of Quebec, but their price after shipping charges to Montreal are deducted is only 23J or 24 cents. In producing at 24 cents, which is supposed to be the optimum or the best they can do, those who know the situation and their societies argue that they are losing money. Of course they understand that it is a temporary measure of support. They hope, possibly more than I could, that the situation will be short-lived, but we never know when the embargo will be lifted. They say that in the meantime the price should be raised to 28 cents at least. They
Agricultural Products-Floor Prices want 30 cents, but as good traders- and farmers are good traders-they will accept 28.
In fact they accept 26 cents and say that it is much better than the way they were treated after the first war when there was no floor. Some of them argue that floors were inevitable because at one time a ceiling was also imposed. That is quite so, but most of them understand that the ceiling was imposed generally throughout the country on all commodities during the war, and if they would compare how they fared during the war and what they had as the result of their dealings under the ceiling system they understood they were a lot better at the end of last war than at the end of the first war when there were no ceilings on any commodities.
As I said, I felt a little awkward in getting up to speak on this subject, but the main object of my representation is to ask the minister to consider the special situation facing eastern farmers and particularly those of Quebec. You cannot it is true treat one part of the country differently from another but nevertheless there are differences in support prices between the various parts of the country because of shipping and other factors that are taken into account. However, because of the local facilities I think special consideration should be given to the Quebec farmers.
There is another point on which they want representations to be made. They fear that the floor on butter, which is 58 cents at the present time, may not be kept at that level. Some of them maintain that it should be raised to 62 cents. Some of them say that in a speech of the minister or some official of the department a price of 62 cents was promised at one time. It has not been shown to me and I do not know about it, but at any rate they fear that the floor price might go below 58 cents. The importation of buiter last winter from outside countries can be explained to them. It has not been properly explained to them by some of their own associations, and I will come to that point in a moment. There had been a shortage in the previous winter. In order that this situation would not arise a second time the government thought it wise to import a certain quantity of butter from the Scandinavian countries.

If I might be permitted to interrupt, it might be well for me to raise this matter at this point in my hon. friend's speech. The floor price is set for another year at 58 cents. There is no question about that. It is 58 cents for another year.

Agricultural Products-Floor Prices

I thank the minister, and if I ever send out reprints of my speech he can be sure of having justice accorded to him. I thank him for the correction. It is human nature not only with farmers hut with everyone else to try to have a better life, and these people have asked for a floor of 62 cents. I am quite sure if I go back to them and say that the minister has stated that the floor has been extended for another year it will give them great relief.
Maybe I should put the statement correctly. A year ago the floor was set at 58 cents for two years, and it runs for another year.
And ends when?
About a year from now, the first of May, 1953.

Then they are not only misinformed but they have misinformed me because I know nothing of the matter. The fact is that their own associations circularize them with respect to such things. The people concerned are requesting a subsidy on the [DOT]transport of feedstuffs to reduce their costs [DOT]of raising hogs or a higher ceiling on bogs f.o.b. Quebec for the eastern part of Quebec.
I should like to touch on a circular letter sent out by a Quebec farm organization and entitled, "An open letter to federal members". If I voice the desires of these people, who after all constitute 95 per cent of my constituents, if I take a great interest in their fate, try to understand their problems and be their voice and true representative in parliament, I must also point out that there are certain inaccuracies which their own associations have tried to instil into their minds.
When some people want to ask for something they start out by insulting or threatening, by using strong words of abuse or reproach in the hope that it will make their position stronger. I have discussed this open letter to federal members at the last four gatherings I have had in my constituency. These people are all interested in mixed farming. Some are small farmers, some are larger than others, and most of them are members of these associations. This paper is called La Terre de Chez Nous, and it is published by the Union of Catholic Farmers. I think that most farmers should belong to an association so that their interests can be looked after. I know that this association has sided most of the time with the opposite party provincially and federally, or rather it has been against everybody in authority but nevertheless I would advocate that the
tMr. Gardiner.]

farmers join the association because it is their only means of putting forward their views. I do not disapprove of their belonging to it or making it stronger. They might choose their officers and the editors of their paper a little more carefully, but in any event this paper, which has quite a large circulation throughout the province, has published this open letter to federal members which I feel I must take to task.
I am not going to take very long to comment on it. I read all the numbers of this paper because even if I am not an expert on the problems they deal with I feel it is my duty to do so, and I read each number when it arrives. The first statement I do not like begins with these words:
You who are in parliament where crises are made and who do not realize they are made . . .
Crises are not made in parliament. The crisis of the moment in a certain field of agriculture was not made in parliament. If Great Britain does not have enough funds to carry on purchasing in the dollar area and has to revert to the sterling zone, is that a crisis made in parliament? I think it is utterly false to say a thing like that. If the United States government felt that it was their duty to their own cattle raisers and to their population generally to impose an embargo because Canada had foot-and-mouth disease in the west, I think that nobody can say frankly, fairly and honestly that it is a crisis made in parliament. On the contrary, from the first moment the government tried to deal with it so that remedies may be brought about and help given where it was needed and members of parliament knew what was going on. Because the epidemic occurred in western Canada, most of the western members spoke on the subject. I did not think it was the proper time for eastern members, since no cases had been found in that part of the country, to enter the debate. Until the consequences of this outbreak were felt in the eastern part of Canada, it was quite proper to give the floor to those members who, for many days, talked about the matter.
Then this paper goes on and says that during the war the government-and in this they try to bank on the feelings of a small part of the community; they try to bank on some sentiments that they still hoped to find here and there in some districts of Quebec-they say that during the war the government in order to feed Britain made the people bear the full brunt of controls, even to the point of depriving Canadians of their needed food. That is a false statement, and as I told this meeting last Sunday, "I do not know of any of you in this room who got any thinner or whose health got

any worse during the war." This country's controls were applied fairly to the largest number of people. If the people fared so well during the war it was because, as the minister mentioned a moment ago, we were buying much larger quantities of farm products, building new industries and giving more salary to the men in industry. This was done by taking from people, corporations and so on who could afford to pay, the amounts needed for these purchases. Most people understand that such appeals no longer are effective in Quebec, yet here you see them and they are circulated to 50,000 people. I believe, therefore, it is worth while to talk about this matter.
A little farther on this paper oblivious of what happened during the war says that it is the poor farmer who has been the victim. In succession they say he has experienced the invasion of margarine, the fall in the price of hogs, the epidemic of foot-and-mouth disease, the United States embargo, the importation of butter from other countries and the fall to the lowest level of the prices of butter and cheese. First of all, the invasion of margarine was not a crisis which was made in the federal parliament. There was a law on our statute books preventing the manufacture of that product. The government felt it was their duty, rather than see one group of people in the country taking the matter to the Supreme Court of Canada and trying to secure something which the other group felt should not be given, that is a declaration of the federal law as being ultra vires, to refer this matter to the supreme court. I believe the government acted quite properly. The decision of that court was in favour of the provinces, so in some provinces margarine was manufactured. Quebec imposed a ban on it but the ban was ineffective in a way because it was called a spread or went under another name, so it was kept on the market. However, that condition is not something which was fabricated in the federal parliament.
I turn now to the fall in the price of hogs. As I said, this was caused by the closing of the British market, the epidemic and the United States embargo. Those are the three reasons for the decline in price and the farmers know it. Yet in order to make the case against the government even worse this paper goes on itemizing the causes and effects as being all the causes of the unrest that might be felt in certain quarters.
They go on and say that they ask us to speak louder and with more courage in the House of Commons. 1 do not believe anyone in this house can say that the members from Quebec who represent these people have not
Agricultural Products-Floor Prices made representations to the proper authorities when the circumstances warranted. I believe the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) will say that as soon as the outbreak of this disease occurred a number of members from Quebec districts went to see him and bothered his secretaries and his experts in order to obtain the proper data and to be in a position to understand the situation. As hon. members know in order to correct a situation members do not have to get up and speak during a debate as often as some groups may believe they have to do. I do not disapprove of their doing so, but a case can be built quite strongly without ten people getting up and expounding the same theory. It is not the number of representatives from certain parts of Canada who take part in a debate that brings about remedies. One or two representatives making some suggestions would have the same effect upon the minister. When one or two members bring these questions to the attention of the government the effect is the same as if twenty members occupied the already crowded time of this house when some members are desirous of dealing with other matters.
Now, Mr. Speaker, this paper goes on and asks what their members are doing and what they are saying. This is why I am speaking now. What I am doing and saying now may not be the work of an expert in agriculture, but I thought I should make these representations to the minister. I had also to tell these people who are publishing this paper that they are prejudicing the case of the farmers in Quebec and that they cannot justify most of their accusations against the government or the officials of the department. If these people had come forward and said to the government, "Owing to special circumstances in our district, Mr. Minister, we would like more help, higher prices or higher subsidies; we thank you for what you have done but you might do a little more," they might have received a better hearing. Such an approach would have been more sincere and fairer to everybody concerned. But no, there are some people-these people have been doing it for years-who try to arouse feeling between the workers and the farmers, and between the latter and other classes of society, who try to destroy the confidence the farmers have in the government and the federal Department of Agriculture. This has been done by stating that all the federal government does is for the western members because the western members are always speaking on behalf of their provinces.
1 believe that our farmers have more sense than that, Mr. Speaker. However, when you consider that these statements are spread to
