50,000	people I feel it is time for me to get up and voice my disapproval of those tactics.
These people end the article by stating that the farmers of Quebec "hope you will take them out of this crisis created by your government." They try to pin on the government the blame for the foot-and-mouth disease, the United States embargo, the curtailment of British purchases, but frankly, Mr. Speaker, I know, from the courtesy shown by farmers in general, that they appreciate the situation better than this paper does. With his knowledge of the situation and the representations made by members the minister I know will consider any remedy that should be tried. These farmers may feel that, whatever the situation is, they have in Ottawa a department which will give their interests the consideration to which they are entitled.

Mr. Speaker, I always enjoy listening to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner). While I do not often agree with him, I enjoy his speeches. I do not think anyone can make a black picture look rosier than he can. In fact he would put John Fisher to shame if it came to giving a commentary on something that was black and which he wanted to paint white. He is an asset to the Liberal party. They ought to be proud of him, because he gets them out of many holes.
And to the Dominion of Canada.

Look; I want to know who is making this speech. My friends here tell me I do not need your help, though you come from Manitoba; I am quite able to stand on my own two feet.
The minister had something to say about the packers and what a co-operative bunch they were, that they had come to the assistance of the government at this time. That is very good, but it will not keep me from criticizing the packers in future. I have always criticized the packers, and I feel quite justified in doing so. I am going to keep on doing that, because some of the greatest gains the packers ever made came through the misfortunes of the farmers. I need not go into details to tell the farmer members of this house what I refer to. We are in an emergency now, and just wait; you will see how the packers will take advantage of it. It does not matter to a packer whether he is paying one cent or 30 cents a pound; he has the same toll for every animal that goes through his plant.
Then the minister said that Manitoba could help by taking the cattle in there. I think the drawback in that connection is that the stockyards at St. Boniface are quarantined. Is that not the trouble?
No, they are not quarantined in the ordinary sense of the word.
They are quarantined in the sense that if tomorrow they took Saskatchewan animals to kill, which they would be quite willing to do, they could not get rid of the beef.

Oh, yes, they could. There is nothing to prevent the meat passing beyond Winnipeg, except the regulation in Montreal under which they do not accept meat from Saskatchewan, but I think that will be cleared out of the way in due course.
I thought it was a federal quarantine on the yards there.
No, there is no quarantine on meat going through.
But there is a quarantine on the yards?
Saskatchewan cattle have always been killed at Winnipeg, but now Manitoba says they cannot be killed there. That is the obstruction.
What is the effect of the federal quarantine on the situation in Winnipeg?
The federal quarantine says that live animals cannot go past Winnipeg. Under our quarantine live animals can go into Winnipeg and be killed, but the Manitoba government says they cannot.

This problem has pointed up what I have advocated in the house on other occasions, the need for a board of livestock commissioners. If we had such -a board today I believe it could handle this situation. It would be able to regulate the traffic, and do it on a federal basis, because it would have that power. Of course when I brought up the matter in 1944 the minister pointed out that it would not be legal. He said it would be similar to the board of grain commissioners, which at that time he said we just tolerated, that if it went to a legal battle we would lose out. But if we had that board of livestock commissioners today we would have an organization to deal with this emergency. The next time I made the suggestion the objection was that the farmers did not want it. At that time I was able to show that every farm organization has asked for such a board for the last forty years.
Coming back to the floor prices, I have here a copy of the Western Producer of May 8, 1952, and I am going to quote from page 4:
Pool livestock men pointed out that the federal government had not made any arrangements to

take beef from Manitoba and Saskatchewan packing plants at the floor price. Government statements cited the continuance of the Manitoba embargo on cattle shipments from Saskatchewan, together with the absence of sufficient cold storage space in Saskatchewan, as reasons for the government's refusal to buy at the floor price in these provinces.
Pool officials concluded, therefore, that maintenance of the floor price depended entirely upon the success of the government's request that farmers voluntarily hold back deliveries, especially of feeder cattle which could stand further finishing on pasture.
But, the pool men declared, the hold-back request could not be expected to work, for two reasons: One, pressure to deliver cattle would increase following seeding, especially since more farmers than usual had fed cattle over the winter; and two, because failure of the federal government to require all cattle marketings be made through public stockyards simply meant that there would be greater direct-to-plant deliveries by farmers.
They go on and deal with prices, but I need not read that because it has been read here two or three times. We have these floor prices which the minister has said cannot be enforced. I do not know why. What is the good of putting in floors if you cannot enforce them? The prices have been set too low anyway, as was pointed out by the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Ross) and the other three hon. members who spoke. Even so the packers will not pay those prices, and it seems absurd to set prices which the packers need not pay. There should be some way of overcoming that. There are enough lawyers in the house to find some means of making the packers pay the prices they should pay.
These prices are $25 at Toronto, $23.25 at Saskatoon, $22.80 at Calgary, $22.55 at Edmonton and $23.40 at Vancouver. I am quite sure the minister has always erred on the low side in setting prices. He has admitted that himself; I need not debate that with him. Yet here the packers are chiselling another dollar or two beyond that. I think that is bad, and something should be done about it.
Another point is this business of setting the price for a month or two months ahead. I have spoken here in the house on forward prices, but I never took that to mean a month, six weeks or two months ahead. I figured that when we set forward prices we meant for three or four years ahead so that farmers would have some stability and security and would know where they were going.
Coming back to the floor prices, if ever there was an emergency, this is one. The government should give us the benefit of that legislation and enforce it. If they do not, I just hate to think what is going to happen to the farmer.

If my hon. friend will permit me, it has been mentioned two or three times that the price is fixed for only a month. It is longer than that. The present price is set until July 1, and that would be about three months from the time it was first announced. Well, on June 1 the price is determined for the month of July and from *then on it is determined from month to month; but it is always for two months ahead. I should like to suggest that it is not only possible that it will go down; it is possible that it will go up. It is an adjustment of the prices. There is no doubt that if we had not been able to make the British agreement it would have gone down, but with the British agreement made I do not know which way it will go.
That is no guide to the man who is going to breed a cow for the future.
It is more of a guide than he ever had before, and he has been breeding cows a long time.

You keep coming back all the time telling us that this is the best government; and that you have done more for agriculture than any other body. You have not even brought in any forward prices yet. What benefit or what stability has the farmer? The farmer has no more stability today under the Liberal government than he had under the Tory government. The sooner you wake up-
He is in a bad way, then.

I might tell you this in all sincerity. The farmer will never go back to the mere pittance that he got for his work before the war. He will fight as he never fought before for something better than he had before.
Agricultural prices were the last to go up, and were the first to drop. They are going back now, and the government is doing very little about it, in order to keep them up. Take the position of the farmer today. In approximate figures he is taking $80 to $100 less for a steer than he was in February. I am sure the Minister of Agriculture will agree with me that there is that drop. Take a hog; he is taking about $35 for a hog that he was getting $54 and $55 for. How much has the consumer benefited by that?
Plenty.
The consumer is getting no benefit from that.
Who said "plenty"?
I did.

spareribs?

I shall continue to vote the way I wish, not the way some people to my right vote.
Yes, you told me that.

The minister in January of this year actually promised the cheese producers that he would set a floor price under cheese. How long is it going to take the minister to fulfil that promise? The situation has worsened since that time; still nothing has been done.
I never make any promises.

The cheese producers of this country were waiting patiently until the last two or three weeks, but they are rather impatient today. The minister made the suggestion that there was going to be a meeting tomorrow. I would hope that some good would come out of it, and that the minister would set a reasonable floor price for cheese. He made the statement today that Ontario was the only province that produced a surplus of cheese. We hope that that is not going to be used against us in the setting of the floor price.
The minister made some comments regarding the amount of talking done, and its effect on the price of beef today. I think it has been made plain enough and obvious enough to all people across Canada that, no matter if beef is slightly infected with foot-and-mouth disease, it does no harm so long as it is cooked properly. So I do not think there has been much reduction in the consumption of beef in this country, as a result of any talking done here from either side of the house.
I say that the floor price legislation has been nothing but a farce and a hoax to the agricultural producers of this country. It has won for the Liberal party two elections; and, apart from that, I can see very little that has come from it.
Butter producers are the only group who have received anything near the actual floor set by the government for their product. In other cases the floor price is set to the wholesaler, and the producer in some cases gets a small proportion of it. It has no relationship whatever to the cost of production. The floor price is a guarantee only to the wholesaler, not to the producer.
There never has been a formula written into the act. Although the minister claims he has a formula, and that he works upon it, that formula does not always bear out what has been said. That is particularly true


when we keep in mind the figures that were given this afternoon by the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch). I will admit the minister made a very good try today to paint a rosy picture-and that is something he does very well. But the floor price now set on beef, for a period of two months, is of very little use to any producer. It does not give him any security. He has no idea what the floor price will be after the two months are up.
I will say now that it is not only the farmer who will lose by this fact. Eventually the consumer will pay a higher price for his product because the floor price is not set high enough to hold production. In that way production will be lowered, with the result that the consumer will pay more for the product than otherwise he would have done if the floor price had been kept at a reasonable level so as to keep production where it should be.
I say again that the price to the producer has gone down considerably more than the price to the consumer. The fact that the floor prices are not high enough to keep production at a proper level will mean that the consumer will be the one who eventually will have to pay for the government's delinquency.
May I ask a question?
Yes.
What was the top price paid to hogs-
Oh, oh.
Just hold yourself, now. What was the top price paid for hogs in any of the five years between 1930 and 1935 when the Conservative government was in power.
I think the hon. member will agree that the top price paid for anything between 1930 and 1935 was not anywhere near the top price paid today.
Answer the question. What was the top price paid?
I do not have to answer it.
It would embarass you and your opposition.

Mr. Speaker, I shall not be long in what I have to say. I would bring before the house one point which I believe has not been touched upon, or has not been emphasized sufficiently in relation to this matter of meat prices, floor prices and the marketing of stock. I am very pleased indeed to know that some arrangement has been made for the sale of some of our meat to the United Kingdom,

through the co-operation of New Zealand. That is something we should appreciate within the commonwealth organization. The amount that we are likely to sell at the moment is relatively small and the basis upon which the trade is made is temporary and emergent from our point of view.
As the minister knows, I have always felt and I have always said that our main market for farm products throughout the years has been and will have to continue to be the United Kingdom. I criticized the government at the close of the war in 1946, 1947 and 1948 because we had entered into effective arrangements with the United Kingdom to take certain quantities of our meat products, and in not one of those years had we fulfilled the understanding-I will not call it a contract or agreement-that we had with Great Britain. Consequently to some extent -I shall deal with what I think is the other side in a moment-the loss of that market was due to our inability to fulfil the obligations we had undertaken at least tentatively. I have the figures before me for those years but I shall not repeat them because I think I placed them on the record some time ago.
The other reason was that in our undue haste to put into effect the Geneva agreements that were made in 1947 we to some extent prevented the United Kingdom from obtaining Canadian dollars by the sale of British products in the Canadian market. I think we can all recollect that we agreed to wipe out certain wartime tariff concessions to the United Kingdom as at July 1, 1948. The result was that to some extent the ability to earn Canadian dollars with which to buy our farm products was denied to the United Kingdom.
I believe that the only sure and stable market we can have in the future is the United Kingdom. I have been in this country now for 43 years during which time I have been in the prairie provinces. From time to time we have had a good market in the United States for our livestock but whenever livestock and other farm production in that country reached the point where they could supply their own market as we have recently found again we always had difficulty in marketing our livestock and farm products there. That has been the history in this country. We have had embargoes and restrictions placed against our cattle, as well as against other farm products. We have been faced with duties against our wheat, grain and other products.
I believe that if we are going to have longterm and assured markets for our farm products we shall have to look again across

If we are to do that we shall have to enable the customers of Canada to earn enough dollars to pay for our products or enable them to settle their obligations to us in some other way.
I am quite certain that the policy of marketing in North America, that of Canada and the United States, is wrong. The United States and Canada are willing to sell to the rest of the world, but we raise tariff and other barriers against goods that might come into the country and thus enable those overseas countries to earn the necessary dollars to pay for our goods. In other words, you cannot have one-way traffic, you have to have reciprocity as between your customer and yourself if you are going to stabilize the market.
I rose mainly to say to the minister that now that we have started once again the flow of meat by this arrangement I hope that it will be possible to expand the United Kingdom market. Mexico is again entering the United States market. The population of cattle and hogs in the United States has increased in the last two or three years. Of course it will be said that their human population has increased also and therefore they need more of these things, but whenever pressure has been exerted by the farm bloc of the western states we have found it difficult to market our dairy, meat, grain and other products in the United States.
After all the reliable consuming countries are those countries which can produce only sufficient food to feed themselves for three or four months out of the year. It seems to me that this house, this government and this country should be giving some study to the fiscal and tariff policies of our country in an effort to encourage those trade relationships which I think offer the final answer to some of our problems.
Our own domestic consumption should be increased to the greatest extent possible. I am not saying that the minister and others are not of the opinion I have just expressed, but I did think that when we were dealing with floor prices we should be considering ways of putting this trade on a long-term basis. Our farmers have always asked for stability rather than high prices. I have heard the minister say that in this house on numerous occasions. This afternoon the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Bryce) spoke of forward pricing.
Forward pricing is no longer an experiment in the realm of agricultural production. We have seen it undertaken successfully in

Agricultural Products-Floor Prices many countries. It has been undertaken in the United Kingdom. As the minister knows, my relatives in the old land are and have been engaged for generations in the raising of cattle. My father fed cattle. When I was over there three years ago I found farmers to be more prosperous than they had ever been. The reason they gave me was that they knew what they were going to get for their livestock for three or four years in advance. They knew what they were going to get for their poultry products and for other things for months in advance. They had something of a guarantee of production and price stability.

The situation is different with regard to some of the other products we have been discussing this afternoon. The point I am making is that we need a stable market in order to deal with this problem. If I may interrupt, I know my hon. friend-

Boundary Pipeline Corporation and no debt incurred for Canada. Mr. Chairman, I have opposed other pipe line bills similar to this in other years, just as I have opposed this one in the committee of which I was a member. The members of this group opposed these bills on the ground that we believe pipe lines such as these, which are destined to become public utilities and are to be used for the distribution of natural resources, should be built and operated by a public body.
The gas which this company proposes to transport is, to begin with, a natural resource, and it is the opinion of this group that our natural resources should not be turned over to private enterprise for the making of profit, but that they should be used in the best economic interest of the public. The transportation of gas is in a class with hydro; it becomes extremely important in the economic development of the country. Eventually, if this pipe line is built, industry will come to

Boundary Pipeline Corporation depend upon the gas transported by this company; private home owners will come to depend upon it; and the industrial development of those sections of the country through which the line passes, and where gas is available, will be determined to a large extent by the price and availability of this natural resource. We feel that such an enterprise is of far too great importance in the economic life of our country to be exploited primarily in the interests of dividends on invested capital. We feel that the aim of such a service should be to assure the best economic interests of industry and consumers. We feel that the distribution of this natural resource should be geared to the public need, and that providing for that need should be a first consideration.
For years past we have been handing over the natural resources of this country to capitalist enterprise for exploitation without a great deal of regard for the future needs of this country, and without too much regard for the extent to which those natural resources are used to meet the needs of the community. We feel that these resources belong to all the people. We feel that only a government responsible to those people can exploit those resources in the best interests of the people. Had Sir Adam Beck, for instance, and his supporters followed, in the matter of the hydro development in Ontario, the policy which we are following here in the matter of these pipe lines, Ontario would have been deprived of the great publicly-owned hydro system. Ontario industry and Ontario development would undoubtedly have been handicapped since our hydro developments would have been used primarily in [DOT]the interests of investors rather than in the interests of the development of the economic life of the province.
The transportation of natural gas is, in many respects, on a par with railway transportation. I think it is high time that we ceased handing over natural resources to capitalist enterprise in the first place, and leaving it in the hands of capitalist enterprise until such time as they become unprofitable for such interests to operate, then unloading them on the taxpayers of the country. We have done that in several instances, and in our opinion it is a much better policy for those resources, in the first instance, to be developed and controlled by public ownership. It is only good business sense, I suppose, that the first interest of a company such as the one proposing to build this pipe line should be the investors in that company, and the payment of dividends that accrue to those investors.

Granted, of course, that this enterprise becomes a public utility; granted that the dividends here are limited as they are in all public utilities; nevertheless, no company such as this can place public interest first. I know that in the committee the promoters of this company tried to assure us that their sole concern was to supply the people of Manitoba with natural gas; they said that their chief interest in building this pipe line was to make gas available to the people of Manitoba and particularly those of Winnipeg.
I do not think that any of us here are so naive as to believe for a moment that such a company is primarily interested in serving the province of Manitoba with natural gas. As I have said, it is only good business that this company's first interest should be the protection of the investors in the company and the payment of dividends on that investment. It seems to us that here, in the building of pipe lines, is one instance which, probably more than most enterprises that come before us, should be under public ownership.
It may be, of course, that that which serves the best interests of the investors in this country will at the same time serve the best interests of the communities that are to be served by those resources. I think however that history has shown us in numerous cases that the interests of dividend seekers and the interests of the community that is to be served by public utilities do not always coincide. That which is in the best interests of the investors in such an enterprise as this is not necessarily in the best interests of the community. What may in many instances be most profitable in the interests of the community is not of necessity most profitable for the investors in such a public utility enterprise.
There are few people today living in Ontario who would agree to handing over the Ontario hydro system to any private enterprise. Nevertheless when that enterprise was first initiated there were those supporters of free enterprise who fought to retain hydro, just as the supporters of free enterprise are fighting today to secure and retain control of these pipe lines.
There is another question that arises in my mind out of the scramble of companies to secure charters for the building of pipe lines, and I have raised that question on a number of occasions in committee. Just why are so many of these companies joining in the scramble for charters to build pipe lines? When I asked that question of the promoters of this company, I was told that a charter would be valueless to them, would be nothing but a liability to them, unless they eventually

secured from the Alberta government and from the board of transport commissioners the right to build and the right to export gas from Alberta to Manitoba.
I just cannot see astute businessmen going to the expense that is involved in securing one of these charters, in surveying routes, and all the other preliminary expenses, when it is an accepted fact by all these promoters that the very nature of this industry is such that not more than one pipe line will be built to serve any one section of the country. The investment is of such a nature that it would not be economically feasible to build two or more parallel pipe lines through any section of the country. It was generally agreed that one or the other of those applying for charters would eventually secure from the board of transport commissioners the right to proceed with their pipe line, but not two or three of them.
I have no way of proving that my suspicion is based on fact, but I have a suspicion that each one of these companies expects to be in a position to make some use of that charter and to regain with profit every dollar that they have invested in securing that charter, in surveying the route and in any other preliminary expenses connected with it. If that is the case, it will be the consumers of this product who will, in the long run, pay that cost. For every one of those charters that are granted and are not used, the consuming public will eventually pay. On that ground I still fail to see why there is any necessity for granting charters to so many of these companies.
There is another point which causes grave concern as far as this particular company is concerned. This company proposes to build a comparatively short pipe line-that is, short in comparison with the line proposed to be built by other companies-and one with pipes of relatively small dimensions, to carry Alberta gas as far east as Winnipeg. We were given statistics to show that in the opinion of the promoters there was a sufficient market to make that particular pipe line a paying proposition. We were given statistics to show just how much gas would be purchased by industrial firms in the area through which the pipe line passed, by home owners and so forth. But there is reason to believe-and in my opinion good reason-that the estimates provided to us were somewhat exaggerated. There appears to be good reason to believe that the market which will be available for that comparatively short pipe line will not be nearly as large as we were told it would be. Out of that fact arises this situation. In the event of that particular pipe line not proving to be economically feasible, or in the
Boundary Pipeline Corporation event of development showing that that market is not sufficient to make this pipe line a paying proposition, it would then be only good business for that company, in order to make their enterprise a paying proposition, to run from that trunk line spur lines into the United States.
I fail to see where we have any assurance that, once this undertaking is initiated, gas will be made available in Canada or to purchasers in Canada. It seems quite reasonable to assume that once having built the pipe line to Winnipeg and finding that that pipe line is a paying proposition, the most businesslike course to follow would be to build short lines from their main line into the United States, in which case the United States would be getting a supply of Canadian gas before Ontario and Quebec would have access to it.
Many of us on the committee felt that that was a real danger. It is said of course that, in such an event, arrangements could be made with the United States whereby Ontario and Quebec would get an equivalent supply of natural gas to make up for the Canadian gas that was going into the southwestern states. There is no assurance whatever that we can make any such arrangement. As a matter of fact, the opposite is more likely to be true. I hold in my hand a report from the Canadian information agency of Ottawa, dated April 26, 1951, in which it is pointed out that the natural gas industry is finding in the United States that new discoveries are not keeping pace with production. The report goes on to say:
The ratio of reserves to production, according to the American gas association, has dropped from 32-49 in 1946 to 2617 in 1950. The figures show also that the increase in reserves in the continental United States was almost negligible for the year 1950.
In the southwest producing areas, the feeling is growing, according to the federal power commission, that their principal energy resource is being sold out from under them. The commission made this observation in considering applications by natural gas suppliers to serve the New England market.
There is other evidence to show that we cannot proceed on the assumption that if Canadian gas is exported to the United States before Canada's needs are supplied we can be assured of an equivalent supply of natural gas from the United States for eastern Canada.
We are told of course that by opposing this bill, and the incorporation of this company, we will probably be depriving Manitoba and the city of Winnipeg of natural gas for a long time. The argument is used that there is now or will be shortly a sufficient supply of Alberta gas to provide Manitoba with what it needs, but there will not be for some time

Therefore those of us who oppose the granting of this charter are charged with depriving the Manitoba people of access to that gas until more is available for eastern Canada.
In the first place, there is no assurance of course that the province of Alberta will permit the export of gas to Manitoba until there is a sufficient quantity available to warrant the building of larger and longer pipe lines. In the circumstances, I think we in this house must be concerned with the economy of Canada as a country rather than the economy of any one province. I think we in this house must take the long view of this matter and act in the best interests of Canada.
Then we are told of course that this matter can be left to the board of transport commissioners; that in the final analysis they will judge whether this company should get permission to build that pipe line or not. It is the duty of the House of Commons, and not that of the board of transport commissioners, to decide what policy is in the best interests of Canada. The promoters who came before the committee assured us that, as far as the board of transport commissioners were concerned, the one thing they would have to be assured of was that the company was financially capable of building that pipe line, and that there was a market available for the gas they were to supply.
There is no question about the board of transport commissioners' responsibility in determining policy. That is not their responsibility. If we in this house grant a charter to this company, then the concern of the board of transport commissioners is to see that the company is financially capable of doing the job for which the charter was granted. It is our responsibility here to decide whether we want one or a dozen charters granted. It is our business here to decide whether we want one province served at the expense of other provinces, because it is quite evident that the building of this pipe line and the supplying of natural gas to Manitoba will delay the building of the larger pipe line which would service Ontario and Quebec.

Alberta will decide that.

Alberta will decide when and in what quantities natural gas shall be


exported. I doubt whether we in this House of Commons should throw upon the government of Alberta the responsibility of deciding which of those companies granted charters by the parliament of Canada should be chosen. That province will be able to take care of those matters very efficiently. I would be loath to see any export of gas from Alberta until our own requirements are taken care of. Then my view is that British Columbia and Saskatchewan should have the next right of access, and then Manitoba. If we have enough left I would even go so far as saying that Ontario should have some, although they have never done very much for western Canada. I think I shall vote for the bill.

Mr. Chairman, I am glad to have this opportunity to follow the last three speakers, with whom I entirely disagree. Being an Irishman I can safely take that stand and back it up. I was amazed to hear the last speaker say that Ontario should not receive Alberta gas-
I did not say they should not.
-until-
That is better.

-someone in Alberta sees fit to decide that the pipe line company which is incorporated is permitted to take Alberta gas. Let me tell the hon. member who just resumed his seat that I come from Ontario.
Don't apologize.

I hear the hon. member for Comox-Alberni say something. I still wish he would get a constituency which a white man can pronounce. When I hear a statement like that made by a member from Alberta I wonder if he realizes where the money came from that created the oil potential they have in that province.
It did not come from Ontario, do not make any mistake about that.
As I recall what happened in the last few years in Ontario, in Canada and in this house, I remember that Imperial Oil Limited spent about $30 million in Alberta before they struck oil and gas.
That is not Ontario.

It happens that that company has its head office in Ontario and its refinery

in my city. I do not want to hear this chirping from my left that Ontario has made no contribution to Alberta. The hon. member should go back and find out just who it was that developed Ontario with respect to oil and gas.
Not Ontario.

Alberta. I hope I did not make any mistake in that. There are different aspects to this matter but I have not sufficient time tonight to develop them all. I think as Canadians we all share in the natural resources of this country whether they are found in Newfoundland, Alberta, Ontario or any other place. As administrators for the people of the Dominion of Canada I think it is up to us to see that those resources are developed for the benefit of Canadians generally. Since I came to this house I have never taken a provincial attitude with respect to the development of natural resources, nor can I recall that many other members have. Unfortunately there are a few occasions when we find provincialism.
In this house you have got to stand up for yourself.

I am one who rather resents such provincialism in a country like Canada which is now coming into its own in no small way. With respect to the natural resources of any province, we must concede that the particular province concerned possibly has rights over and above those of the neighbouring provinces. I appreciate the attitude of the government of Alberta in endeavouring to keep within its control and at its disposal sufficient gas to last them over a period of years. However, I do not believe, and I do not think there are many people in the province of Alberta who share the opinion, that they can have their cake and eat it too. I think I share the opinion of most members of this house that it is to the advantage of the province of Alberta to export gas and oil.
I think that the people of this country must make it known to our friends to the south that so far as traffic and trade in these two most vital of our recently discovered natural resources is concerned there must be some mutual understanding which heretofore has not appeared on the surface. I think that in a diplomatic manner it must be made quite plain to the authorities on the other side of the line that we would like to do business in oil and gas with the United States but that we resent the tariff imposed against our oil entering the United States. Up until the discovery of oil in Canada we had to import practically all our
Boundary Pipeline Corporation oil requirements, and I regret to say there are people on the other side of the line who seem to think that they should still be supplying us with all our oil, and who also certainly hold the opinion that no Canadian oil should go into the United States in spite of the fact that for years we have been buying practically 100 per cent of our oil requirements from that country.
I think it is time for our government and the government of the United States to discuss these very important questions. We now find ourselves supplying the state of Montana with some 10 billion cubic feet of Alberta gas per year under a five year contract. I do not think any member of the house has any doubt in his mind as to the extension of the contract when the first five year term expires. It is true that the gas is being exported for defence purposes, and as a member of the team we are justified in endeavouring to see that any defence requirements of our allies that we can fill are supplied without hesitation. At the same time I cannot help but think that we are entitled to a little more consideration so far as two-way trade is concerned with respect to a product so vital to the economy of both countries.
I come from western Ontario where a small amount of Texas gas is obtained. I know we have great difficulty in securing our requirements. We were supposed to get some 5 billion cubic feet per year, and at the present time I think we are only getting 2i billion cubic feet per year. After all is said and done, I am one of those-and I hope that many share the same opinion-who believe that if we are prepared to export 10 million, 15 million or 20 million cubic feet we in turn should be placed in the position where we can obtain a like amount from the United States to be used in areas where the use of that gas would be cheaper to consumers than to bring it from the province of Alberta.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to object most vigorously to the way in which the government is handling, or perhaps it would be truer to say mishandling, the present housing situation.
The number of houses started in the years 1948 to 1950 inclusive remained constant at about 94,000 units per year. In 1951 the

Housing
number of new houses started was 72,000. That is a reduction of 24 per cent during the past year.
No less a person than Mr. Mansur, president of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, has estimated that the number of new houses which will be built during the present year will be between 55,000 and 60,000 units. That means that today we are building 42 per cent fewer houses per year than we were building two years ago.
Why has there been such a sharp reduction in the number of houses built last year, and which are being built this year? I believe it is due largely to the abolition of the one-sixth mortgage loan provision of the National Housing Act.
According to the minister's own statement, as recorded on page 70 of Hansard for February 5, 1951, the abolition of the one-sixth mortgage loan made it necessary, a year ago, for a prospective purchaser to increase his down payment on a five-room minimum house by about $1,000, and a purchaser of a six-room minimum house by about $1,500. Because of the increase in housing costs during the past year, these increases in down payments are at least $1,250 and $1,800 today.
According to the latest report of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, an income of at least $3,300 is required to meet the debt services on a minimum house today. I should like to quote from that report as follows:
On the assumption that an average family cannot afford more than about 23 per cent of its income for shelter, the average prospective homeowner in 1950 required a gross income of about $2,700 to purchase a new minimum house. By the end of 1951, family income of about $3,300 was required to meet the debt service on a similar house.
An income of considerably more than $3,300 is required before the money now required for down payment can be set aside. Because of the abolition of the one-sixth mortgage loan, it is generally agreed that a man must earn at least $5,000 a year, for at least five years, in order to set aside the $2,500 or more which is now required as down payment on a minimum house. This means that people whose incomes are less than $5,000 a year are virtually excluded from buying a new house. This defeats the very purpose of the government's existing housing legislation.
If shortages of materials, caused by our defence program, made necessary a reduction in the number of houses built, then the sacrifices should have been shared as evenly as possible by all social groups. To impose restrictions which made it impossible for those with incomes below $5,000 to buy new
[Mr. Hees.l
houses, and to impose no restrictions whatsoever on those with larger incomes, was completely unfair and unjust. It is a clear case of rationing by the purse.
What has made the situation even worse is that the 200,000 immigrants, whom the government is bringing into the country each year, largely come within the low income group. These people must be housed, and they have simply increased the housing pressure on those who have had new housing denied to them.
And now, what is the situation today? When the government abolished the one-sixth mortgage loan on February 5 of last year, the Minister of Resources and Development said that the government was taking this step to conserve building materials needed for the defence program. The situation today was described by Mr. Mansur's statement that, although there were some limitations upon new residential starts because of shortages of certain types of building materials, this difficulty no longer exists, and he did not believe that, except in very isolated instances, the lack of building materials would play any part in limiting the amount of new residential construction in 1952.
In other words, the reasons which the Minister of Resources and Development cited to justify the removal of the one-sixth mortgage loan, have now disappeared. However, the government persists in denying new housing to those with incomes of less than $5,000. This unjust and unfair discrimination against those who need housing most must be removed immediately.
In the interest of those for whom housing accommodation is most needed, I would ask the government to reconsider its position with regard to its one-sixth mortgage loan arrangements, which it discarded to meet conditions not now existent. In this way, the housing legislation of this country can be made more immediately effective, and brought back in line with its original intent and purpose.
In addition to the large number of people who want to buy a new house, there are many whose greatest need is good rental housing at a reasonable rent. The answer to this problem is the low rental housing project, in which the three levels of government participate in the cost.
In Toronto we have a very excellent example of this kind of housing, in the Regent Park project. Toronto needs at least six of these projects, and I hope that, now that the province of Ontario has taken over the 7J per cent of the cost formerly borne by the

municipalities, Toronto and many other centres will undertake these projects on a large scale.
I hope that other provinces will follow the example of Ontario in assuming the full 25 per cent of the cost, formerly shared by the province and municipality. This relieving of the municipalities of their share of the cost should make it easy for many centres to undertake these low rental housing projects. I believe that they are the only answer to the housing problems of a very large number of Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, the subject of housing is one in which I have always had considerable interest. It was actually not my intention to speak on it at this time, but after listening to some of the speeches which I have heard on housing, and, I say with some generosity, to the superficiality of what has been said on the subject, I think it is time for a little plain speaking on this subject. The hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Hees) has stated that the abolition of the one-sixth additional loan by Central Mortgage and Housing last year was a great error. Who knows, perhaps it was an error. But we all know why it was done. It was done because it was considered at that time there was a shortage of building materials, and that those that were available were necessary for the war effort. If that was wrong, it was an honest mistake and it was quickly remedied.
Now, at the time we had this one-sixth additional loan, the lending value which was used was highly fictitious and very conservative. When we returned into the larger mortgage field after the abolition of the one-sixth mortgage loan, we adopted a more realistic attitude. From October last when the new method was introduced it was an 80 per cent loan based on the selling price and not on the lending value, and 90 per cent for war workers based on the selling price and not on that fictitiously low lending value. Since that time, we have had much greater loans than we ever had before. As a result, the down payments have been decreased on these small houses that come within the category covered by this loan.
I think it should be pointed out also-few people seem to realize it today-that when the dominion government came into this field they came into it gratuitously and to help the Canadian people, not because it was a field they were constitutionally obligated to enter. It was a field that involved property and civil rights-a field which every provincial government, if they are honest, must acknowledge as their sole responsibility. But
Housing
in view of the fact that they were not carrying out that responsibility, the federal government entered into it in 1935 and has continued to this date. And when they are in it all they can do is to provide financial assistance, because we have not the legislative jurisdiction over property and civil rights. We have made that money available, in large quantities, and with the co-operation of the provincial government, under section 35 of the National Housing Act, almost anything can be done under that section.
I would point out, Mr. Speaker, that at this moment if there is one government in this country that has almost completely failed to take any part under section 35, it is the one Conservative government in Canada today in the province of Ontario.
I would point out that last year the attorney general of the province of Ontario made a large announcement that they were going to enter into a scheme with the federal government under section 35 of that act. At that time it was pointed out that they were going to build, I think it was, 10,000 housing units through the province of Ontario which would be given on a population basis throughout the province. At that time, I believe, on the population of the city of Toronto we were entitled to 500 units. It was pointed out that they would be erected on what have been for many years-and still are -the rifle ranges at Long Branch, Ontario.
At the time that announcement was made, anybody who knows anything about the rifle ranges at Long Branch knows that that was an unfortunate statement and, I may say, a misleading one. It has been well known that the Long Branch rifle ranges which are in the township of Toronto are not being given up by the Department of National Defence until the township of Toronto finds some other place which is equally suitable and hands it over to the Department of National Defence. It was known at that time that no such lands had been found, that no such deal had been made; that, if such a deal were made, it could not be made within a year or two; and that the 500 houses which were so glibly published as being on our doorstep had no possibility of being built there for at least a year or two years. I venture to say, Mr. Speaker, that we shall probably never see them on that site.
In every other way the province of Ontario has been very co-operative verbally. Their co-operation has consisted in appointing a housing administrator. I believe that he has an assistant and two stenographers. They have gone into this business in a large way. They have insisted that they are interested

Housing
in housing, and that they are doing everything possible to help us in housing. To date their interest has been extremely volatile and extremely verbal.
Aside from this provincial responsibility which everybody knows exists, and which the provincial government of Ontario has completely and utterly failed to meet, I should like to go into some of the real problems of this housing question. Many of us know what these problems are and they are not just glib talk about the abolition of the one-sixth. There are three main problems, and everyone knows them who knows anything about the building game. The first is the availability of mortgage money. The second is the relationship of lending value and sale price; and the third is the availability of serviced land. Those are the three problems that face anybody who knows something about the matter; I am not professing at all to know everything about it, Mr. Speaker, but I have some slight knowledge of the subject, and I say, with the greatest of deference, that such knowledge does not appear to have been demonstrated in some speeches that I have heard.
These problems must be faced honestly and clearly; they must be faced not with confusion, not with prejudice, but clearly and honestly. The first problem is the availability of mortgage money. The availability of mortgage money is something which depends largely on the lending institutions. The lending institutions are the institutions which have money available, in the same way as has any company depending on the money which comes into their hands through the payments largely of insurance premiums and through the availability of funds from the other securities which are not deemed as suitable at that time as the mortgage loans appear to be for their investment portfolio.
We all know that the insurance companies and various lending institutions have large holdings of government bonds. We all know that the government bonds have gone down in value, and that if the insurance companies are to have large amounts of money to invest in mortgage loans they have to liquidate these bonds at a very considerable loss.
I hold insurance policies as, I presume, does every other member in the house. I am sure that the policyholders of these insurance companies are not anxious to have these companies liquidate their bonds at a loss in order to get into the mortgage field when other fields are equally or more profitable and attractive.
Today on mortgages the lending institutions can get 5J per cent. On many of the

investments in municipal bonds and debentures and commercial bonds and debentures today they can get 4J per cent. Today it is a well-known fact that these National Housing Act loans are expensive to service. There is a great deal of servicing in connection with them. In most lending institutions the cost of that servicing is something over one per cent. Accordingly it is simpler for them to buy these bonds yielding 4J per cent, and it is slightly more profitable for them to do so.
It may be that, as a matter of public duty, the lending institutions of Canada should get into the mortgage field, perhaps in a larger way. Maybe they owe that duty to the people of Canada, but it is not a public service that they owe to their policyholders. In fairness to the lending institutions-and I hold no brief for them-I think it must be stated that most of them are in that field and are making as much mortgage money available for this purpose as is consistent with their financial position.
It must be remembered that during the days of 1949, 1950 and 1951 when they were putting out mortgage money in a large way, they were not putting it out from current revenues alone but were putting it out from current revenues and the conversion of government bonds and other securities into cash in order to make it available for mortgage money. To date they are limited, by reason of the fall of many of their investments in value, to the current revenue coming in from their insurance premiums and other earnings.
I think that is a fair statement of the situation and I think we must face it. I do not think it is fair to ask the lending institutions to place money out at a rate of interest and in a manner which is less profitable to them than is some other manner. If we are going to face the problem honestly, we must acknowledge the fact that if we want them to get into it in a larger way we must be prepared to give them a larger guarantee.
I think we should also cover the relationship of the lending value and the sale price. I shall have something to say on that subject later but I would point out at this moment that we have, under the present regulations under the housing act a more realistic approach. Formerly 80 per cent of the value was calculated on what was called the lending value and that lending value was a fictitious lending value based not on a sale price but on a lower figure which was based on perhaps the sale price some years earlier. To date it is based on actual sale price; and a builder who builds, under this act, certain types of housing with certain sizes of loans, depending on the types of housing

involved-they are all 80 per cent loans except those for war workers which are 90 per cent-knows that when he sells that property at a price which is controlled under the National Housing Act by Central Mortage and Housing Corporation, he is going to get an 80 per cent advance on that actual sale price. It is a much more realistic approach and, I think, a much better one. As I say, I shall a little later have something to suggest in that behalf.
I think one of the most difficult and one of the main problems today-I think it is probably the most important problem today-is the availability of serviced land. In all of the larger urban localities the serviced land has been used. There is practically no serviced land available for housing. By serviced land I mean land that has been serviced with water, sewers, schools and that type of thing. There is just nowhere for people to build on serviced land.
It is a fact well known by builders and others who are acquainted with the subject, that housing subdivisions are not self-supporting in so far as the cost of schooling is concerned. Simply by placing the normal rates of taxes on this housing, the municipality immediately incurs much greater debts and much greater obligations by reason of the costs of schools which will have to be erected in order to meet the needs of the families which come into that housing division.
No municipality today which has had any experience in this field is very anxious to allow large housing subdivisions to be placed within its confines unless at the same time it is getting a fairly large proportion of industry to cover the additional taxation for schooling. So that today, before you can file a plan and get the serviced land in most of the municipalities-I am talking about urban municipalities at this point, Mr. Speaker- you must go to elaborate lengths before getting approval from the planning boards in Ontario, or if there is no planning board in the municipality, from the department of planning and development. You must put in the roads yourself; you must put in the water yourself; you must put in the sewage yourself; you must put in sewage disposal plants yourself; in some cases you must underwrite the cost, or part of the cost of the school building. You have to donate the land for the public and separate school; you have to donate so much land for park land, and it goes on and on; and the restrictions become greater all the time, and the cost greater. It has reached the point today that a small builder has practically no chance of getting serviced land, unless he is fortunate enough
Housing
to be able to get some from some land servicing group. Therefore we are entering into the period when it is the large builder, the large scale builder, who is able to service sufficient land and therefore build enough houses to get enough profit out of them to make it worth his while.
House building today is a very large scale business. It is not the small builder who is doing the work today. If one looks at the number of builders operating in any municipality today he sees that the number has been cut at least in half, and sometimes down to one-third, simply because there is not enough available serviced land to build houses. And the big builder, when he finally goes through all this, complies with all the restrictions, all the regulations, all the necessities, the enormous expenses of filing a registered plan and getting permission to go ahead to build, is not too anxious to sell this land to the smaller builders, because his profit is going to be made not just by servicing the land and selling his serviced land, but by building on it and getting his profit out of the houses to be erected on it. That is one of the great problems today. I may say that that problem has not been met, very definitely has not been met, and it cannot be met until the provinces carry out their duties.
The duty of the province is definitely to assist municipalities to a much larger extent on the question of schooling. The question of schooling is something that today is not being faced, I know, in my own province- I am not so sure how it is being faced in other provinces. I know that in Ontario the provincial government has resolutely refused to face the question of the cost of schooling in the municipality, and until they are willing to face it, they are going to have this continued problem of the lack of serviced land, because the municipalities are definitely not going to permit land to be serviced within their municipalities for housing to any large extent until they get some additional help from the province in meeting the cost of schooling. I put that out because everyone who is in this building business, and anyone who has anything to do with it, is well acquainted with these problems, and realizes that while the dominion government can make money available, they are not in a position to service land themselves without the co-operation of the provinces and of the municipalities. We all know that under section 35 of the National Housing Act the dominion government has made available for servicing land and for building on that serviced land 75 per cent of the cost thereof, and all that the province has to put up is 25 per cent, and with the

Mr. Speaker, I have listened with great interest to the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Hees) who laid the blame for our housing shortage at the door of the federal government, and with equal interest to the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Hunter) who shifted the blame to the provincial government in Ontario.
The fact remains of course that whether it is the fault of the provincial government or that of the federal government, we need houses and we are not getting them. The fact remains that the housing policy of the federal government needs reviewing in the light of present-day needs and present-day circumstances. It seems to me that, regardless of what Ontario has or has not done in the matter of housing-and I hold no special brief for the government of Ontario-the situation has developed today to a point where the federal government should revise the policy which directs Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation.
In an earlier speech I pointed out that particularly during the last year the two most serious obstacles in connection with housing were lack of serviced land and lack of mortgage funds. I realize of course that the provision of serviced land is a matter for the province and the municipalities. I realize, too, that the three-way agreement between the federal government, the provincial government and the municipalities for the acquisition and servicing of land is just not working. It just is not getting the land. It is not making it possible for municipalities to proceed with building on a large scale. I pointed out that the provision of water, the provision of sewers, streets, sidewalks, fire 55704-138J
Housing
protection, parks, playgrounds and especially education, which the building of a large number of houses in a comparatively short space of time places upon a municipality, is a burden that most municipalities cannot bear.
A housing authority is reported in the press only this week as saying that three ol the townships in the Toronto suburban areai would go bankrupt within a few years if they continued to build homes without at the samp time securing industrial development. His: advice was that, to save themselves from bankruptcy, those townships must call a halt to the building of homes until such times as more industries have moved into those townships so as to assist in carrying part of the municipal tax burden the citizens of the townships must bear.
Some assistance must be given to the municipalities by the federal or provincial governments. Either some way must be found of relieving the municipalities of some of the burden they are now called upon to bear in the matter of education and social services, or those municipalities must be provided with a larger share of the tax income. I realize that this comes within the jurisdiction of the province. I feel nevertheless that because housing is of such national importance it becomes the duty of the federal government to show some leadership and to take some initiative in getting together with the provincial and municipal governments to see if some way cannot be found out of this difficulty.
It is said by authorities that the housing situation today is hampering our defence effort. It is certainly retarding production within the provinces and affecting the whole social structure of our society. The housing situation is of such importance that in my opinion the federal government, if it is to carry out its duty to the Canadian people, should assume the responsibility of getting together the governments at the three levels with a view to working out some solution to this problem whereby houses can be provided for those who need them.
This government has persisted in refusing to contribute anything to the ordinary public and secondary school systems within the province. It insists upon leaving that burden for the province and the municipalities. But it also leaves with the municipalities another responsibility that, in my opinion, is the direct responsibility of the federal government; I refer to the matter of taking care of the unemployed employables.
During the last winter we had in Toronto and its suburbs large numbers of unemployed

Housing
employables. The federal government refuses to accept any responsibility for these people, beyond the payment of unemployment insurance. When unemployment insurance ceases, and in those cases where it is not sufficient to enable a man with a family to get by, this government washes its hands of the matter. The provincial government says that it is not its responsibility, but that it is the responsibility of the federal authorities. The result is that the municipality is left with the burden. It has no choice but to accept the responsibility. The provincial and federal governments are far enough removed from those who are in need that they can afford to remain callous to the demands made. The local municipal council is on the spot. It must either provide assistance for those people, or see them hungry or in debt. In the latter instance, where they are obliged to go into debt, local businessmen have to assume the burden.
If this government still refuses to assist in the matter of education, then I say it could assist in the housing situation, so far as suburban municipalities are concerned, if it would assume responsibility for the unemployed employables who occupy these new houses but who, in many cases, become unemployed and do not have unemployment insurance. I say again that in this matter of providing serviced land and the further matter of getting the municipalities to work with the provincial and federal governments, it becomes the responsibility of this government to show some leadership and to arrive at some arrangement whereby the municipalities will be able to bear the load thrown upon them by reason of the building of these houses.
The second serious obstacle to the building of houses during the past year has been the shortage of mortgage funds. Granted that the houses which are built under the National Housing Act are built for the upper third income group, granted that seventy per cent of our people are not receiving sufficient income to warrant the purchase and the carrying of the cheapest houses built under the National Housing Act, nevertheless if builders could satisfy the present market for houses that can be built at today's prices there would be some relief in the housing situation. As I say, the bottleneck has been the lack of mortgage funds. Mr. Mansur in his report for 1951 says:
Experience in 1951 and the prospects for 1952 suggest that sources of mortgage funds in Canada may not be great enough to sustain a long term annual rate of housing starts at the level of 1949 and 1950.
Then he goes on to say:
If for social reasons an annual housing program equal to or greater than those accomplished in

these years is a requirement then it may prove necessary to find additional sources of credit to be made available for mortgages on new residential construction.
I do not think anyone doubts for one moment that for social reasons we need an annual housing program in this country at least as great as that which was carried out in 1949-1950. As a matter of fact most housing authorities are agreed that if we are to meet the actual needs of the people we should have an annual building program greater than the program which was carried out in 1949. There just is no question on that point, that for social reasons we need such a building program.
Since mortgage funds are not available from the insurance companies or the lending institutions there is only one other source. While Mr. Mansur does not mention that additional source there is no doubt that it is either the federal or the provincial government, or both. The fact that there is a shortage is borne out by the statistics contained in the report which indicates that the number of national housing loans in 1951 were 14,918 as compared with 33,934 in 1950. Those 33,934 loans in 1950 were for 42,280 units; in 1951 the loans were for 19,903 units only. In 1950 the mortgage loans amounted to $284,500,000; in 1951 they amounted to $123,700,000. I think those figures indicate that Mr. Mansur is right in insisting that some additional sources of credit must be made available in order to maintain the annual building program required to meet our needs.
I think there is ample evidence that there is still a market for houses that can be built with the assistance of National Housing Act loans. There is still a market for houses costing $8,000,	$10,000 or more. There
appears to be no great shortage of labour or materials and it would appear that there is still a considerable amount of serviced land available for building. I know personally of one builder who has serviced land available on which to build 400 houses. He has been held up for two years because the lending institutions are no longer interested in lending money under the National Housing Act. There are other builders across the country who have serviced land available for building, but that building is being held up chiefly because no mortgage funds are available from the lending institutions.
Whether or not that shortage of mortgage funds is genuine, whether or not it is a shortage artificially created by the lending institutions in order that they may squeeze more profit out of the present housing emergency, I am in no position to say. But certain it is that the lending institutions today

are no longer interested in lending money in sufficient quantities to meet the housing needs of our people under the terms of the National Housing Act. Certain it is that they are not particularly interested in lending money under the National Housing Act to an extent that will maintain a building program of 100,000 houses a year.
It should be borne in mind that when the government set up its housing authority and undertook to guarantee or to secure the lending institutions against loss on money lent for purposes of building, the government provided an outlet for money which the lending institutions did not know what to do with. In the first place the government gave the lending institutions every opportunity to provide that money and build the houses that were needed on their own initiative. Back in 1944 I think the lending institutions set up their own company known as Housing Enterprises Limited. When the finance companies ran into difficulty with their own venture, when they ran into debt, when they found they were unable to build houses at a profit, Central Mortgage and Housing came to their rescue. The government took over that enterprise at a cost of many millions of dollars and rescued the financial institutions from the difficulty into which they had got and Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation is carrying on that enterprise.
Today when those same financial companies find that there are other investment fields more profitable than the building of houses they are just no longer interested. The fact that the nation needs houses means very little to those lending institutions. The government has increased their interest. The government has stepped up the amount of security provided, and I think has made every reasonable opportunity to induce the finance companies to make money available for houses. I think the government has gone much further than it should in seeking to placate the finance companies and to induce them to provide the necessary funds. We have reached a stage now where, as was said by the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll), the lending institutions have vacated that field. To all intents and purposes they have either refused or have been unable to provide the necessary funds to meet the necessary housing program. I think it is high time that the government itself undertook to lend money directly, certainly in communities with over 5,000 population.
As a matter of fact the former president of the national housebuilders association, Mr. Mager, is reported to have said that the insurance companies are attempting to regu-
Housing
late the amount of housing to be built in any one area of Canada. According to a report in the Ottawa Journal of April 8, 1952, he said that the insurance companies even tell them what materials they can use despite what is laid down in the national building code. Then he went on to say that the attitude of the lending institutions amounted to contempt for the government and the building industry generally.
I think if you take that in conjunction with the lobby that the insurance companies carried on last fall when amendments to the Government Annuities Act were before a committee, and the subsequent withdrawal of the measure in compliance with the insurance companies' lobby, one is justified in asking to what extent the insurance companies of Canada control not only Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation but government policy itself. Certainly as far as housing is concerned the hands of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation are tied by government policy, and government policy is working in the interests of the insurance companies rather than in the interests of the hundreds of thousands of people who need houses.
I ask you, Mr. Speaker, what good reason is there why hundreds of thousands of home builders or buyers should be forced to pay insurance companies 5 per cent interest when the government advances the taxpayers' money to these same insurance companies at 3J per cent? What good reason is there except the benefits that accrue to the insurance companies? Why should Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and the Canadian taxpayers have to rely on these companies for mortgage funds? Cannot a government, which can raise $2 billion for national defence, also raise the few millions that will be required to institute and maintain an adequate housing program? Where is the need for the taxpayers of Canada to continue to pay tribute to the Caesars of the insurance world when their own government can provide money for everything else needed by way of services except housing? I submit there is a great need for radical revision of the government's policy both in the matter of direct loans for the building of houses and in the matter of co-operation with provincial and municipal governments with respect to the building of low-cost rental housing.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Beaudoin in the chair.
