The house resumed, from Wednesday, May 7, consideration of the motion of Mr. Claxton that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a bill to amend the National Defence Act to effect certain changes respecting the discipline and administration of the forces and to provide that persons who commit grave breaches of the Geneva conventions of 1949 may be tried out of Canada by court martial; to amend the Defence Services Pension Act to provide that the total emolument, by way of salary and pension, payable to a pensioner who is employed as a civil servant may be adjusted in accordance with current rates of pay and allowances of the forces and to provide that members of the forces who are otherwise eligible for pension may be permitted to count periods of full-time reserve service of a continuous duration of six months or more for the purpose of determining the amount of pension; to amend the Civil Service Superannuation Act to enable a person who served overseas with the Royal Canadian Navy during the second world war otherwise than at sea to count such service for the purposes of the Civil Service Superannuation Act notwithstanding that the time for election to count such service has expired; and to amend the Senate and House of Commons Act to make the provision respecting the eligibility of servicemen to sit as members of the House of Commons consistent with the provisions of the Canada Elections Act.

Mr. Speaker, this resolution introduces a bill to amend four different acts, the National Defence Act, the Defence Services Pension Act, the Civil Service Superannuation Act and the Senate and House of Commons Act. I stated when the debate was last adjourned that it seemed to me to be an unreasonable and unsatisfactory method to introduce amendments to four different acts all under the title of one bill, the Canadian Forces Act, 1952, as the minister intimated it is to be called. My objection to that method is that with amendments to four different measures it might be that exception would be taken to one while the other three would be perfectly satisfactory. One would be in the predicament of having to oppose the bill when introduced 
although one might agree in principle with three of the amendments. The fourth one might not be considered sound and satisfactory. However, that is a procedural matter and I presume that the government has decided to go ahead with that method. I hope it will not become a practice in the future.
Now, regarding the National Defence Act amendment, I understand that will be to provide for the punishment of those who may commit offences against the Geneva conventions, particularly against prisoners of war and injured who have been captured by the enemy. From the minister's remarks I was not quite clear as to who was going to be responsible for the punishment of the offender, because in his remarks he said "regardless of nationality". I do not know whether the punishment will be awarded by some international court or whether it will be awarded by the nation whose servicemen have been captured, and against whom any atrocities may have been carried out. The minister will explain that when speaking, either on the bill or in closing this debate.
I should like to say a few words concerning the amendments to the Civil Service Superannuation Act. I have no comment to make about the amendments to the other acts. Regarding the Civil Service Superannuation Act, it has always been a problem for the retired serviceman to find employment when he has completed his service. Quite frequently his previous training has made his services very valuable to various other departments of the government. Having been in the government service for years, he not unnaturally likes to continue in the public service. Of course, if he has gone into industry, companies have offered to pay for his services according to the value that they may have placed upon them, exactly the same way as provincial and municipal governments do when employing a pensioner.
But for many years the federal government has said that the service pension, plus the remuneration that the pensioner will receive from whatever department he is working in, could not exceed the amount of the pay and allowances that the man received on retirement without affecting his service pension. In the past that applied not only to warrant officers but also to non-commissioned officers and men. This limitation was removed a few years ago so far as non-commissioned officers and men were concerned, but it has remained applicable to officers and warrant officers. I think the amendment that is being introduced is certainly a step forward in the right direction. In view of the fact that service pay has been raised because of the increased cost

of living, the pay of the pensioner will not now be considered as that of the day of his retirement but the pay of the present day. At least, that is my interpretation of the resolution.
I want to point out that I consider that is a step in the right direction, because in the past hardship has existed for pensioners. I should like to put on the record extracts from a letter which I received from a man who served for many years in the old permanent force as a non-commissioned officer, and who subsequently received his commission. I believe this is a typical case. He says:
The most I can draw as a civil servant is $1,550 per annum which, at present, is all taxable to the extent of approximately $280 per annum leaving a net of $1,270. My pension was taxed another $90 making a total tax for 1949 of $370.
I have had to refuse two or three raises from the civil service-statutory increases-even on as low a grading as clerk 2A, as well as the first cost-of-living increase, which might have been granted, including the proposed present increase still pending. If I had accepted them the equivalent amount would have been deducted from my pension.
That letter was dated in February, 1951. The situation in respect to that pensioner will have improved if this amendment is adopted. But I am going to offer the suggestion that we may now remove all the limitations. As it is now, the amendment will work in favour of the higher ranks, whereas the warrant officers, lieutenants and captains who retire will not have the same advantage as those in the more senior ranks. Take the position, for instance, of a captain who retires. His pension, according to whatever length of service he may have, would be based on $389 a month, which is now the pay and allowances of a captain. On the other hand, if a brigadier retires his pension would be based on $930 per month. It is quite obvious, therefore, that the increases would react far more favourably upon the officer in the senior ranks.
You may say that possibly there would not be many junior officers retiring. The class of man who retires as a lieutenant or as a captain would be one who had spent most of his service in the ranks and who had been promoted at the end of his service. He would not have had the opportunity of rising to the more senior ranks. Anyone who retired as a colonel or brigadier or a corresponding rank would have gone in as an officer and throughout his whole service would have been drawing a higher rate of pay. The man in the junior rank would not have had the opportunity of saving as much as the man in the more senior rank. While this amendment will better the conditions of retirement as compared with those which have existed heretofore, I wonder whether
Canadian Forces Act
the time has not come when we can recognize the fact that we have removed the limitation so far as the non-commissioned officers and men are concerned; we are practically removing the limitation so far as the senior ranks are concerned, and in so far as the warrant officers and junior commissioned ranks are concerned, it seems to me we still have a limitation.
If the services of the individual are of value to the civil service, surely the time has come when the civil service can well afford to pay the price for the services which are rendered. I merely ask the minister to give that suggestion consideration before he introduces the bill; and possibly he might see his way clear to remove all restrictions and allow the individual-be he soldier, non-commissioned officer, captain or whether he be in a more senior rank- to receive the pay which the civil service would grant any other individual, without affecting his pension.
May I put it this way. Bear in mind the fact that if he went into civilian life, or if he found employment with a municipal or provincial government, his pension then would not be affected. This provision is placing the junior commissioned ranks and the warrant officer rank at a disadvantage, although I admit quite frankly-and I am pleased to see it introduced-that it is an improvement on the existing system.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I just say a few words? I am sure we have all listened with interest to the points that have been raised by the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes), particularly the matter which he was discussing in the closing part of his remarks. I hope that attention will be paid by the minister to the case that the hon. member has made.
I wish also to support the position taken by the hon. member for Nanaimo wnen he suggests that the government might give further consideration to its method of amending legislation affecting the Canadian forces. Despite an excellent overhaul of the National Defence Act only a few sessions ago, it appears that each session as we meet there are further amendments to be made to the various statutes that affect the Canadian forces.
In addition to the difficulty cited by the hon. member for Nanaimo in connection with this method of having one bill to amend several pieces of legislation, it seems to me that there is also the difficulty that arises in the future as to the problem that will confront those who will look for the complete statute

Canadian Forces Act
in respect of any one of these matters. It seems to me that those who are wanting, for example, to know what is the up-to-date version of the Senate and House of Commons Act or the Civil Service Superannuation Act will be a bit puzzled to discover that, amongst other places, they have to look in amending statutes known from time to time as the Canadian Forces Act. I feel that there is posed by this situation a problem which is [DOT]not solved by this method.
The hon. member for Nanaimo expressed the hope that this pattern would not be followed in the future. This is at least the second time when it has been done. Last year we had a similar bill-I believe it was called by the same name, the Canadian Forces Act-which amended not four or five pieces of legislation but quite a number- seventeen or nineteen-of the statutes of Canada. That was the bill with regard to which we got into a bit of a quarrel with the other house concerning the form of those amendments. The bill as introduced into this house was drafted in rather brief form. The hon. members of the other place thought it should be in much more extended language and they amended the bill accordingly.
I will not pursue the matter further at this time, Mr. Speaker. It is one which involves as well the whole question of what happens to bills like this when the revised statutes are prepared. I simply suggest that further thought might be given to what is the best way to amend a number of statutes in which one department is interested, both from the standpoint of being fair with the house and from the standpoint of being able to find this legislation after it gets on the statute books.

Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to make any detailed statement with regard to the bill at this time. I will save that until the bill is before the house. However, I should like to add my voice to those of the two hon. members who have just taken their seats, and who have made an argument for not including in the one bill the amendments to four separate acts. It seems to me that to do so will cause confusion not only at the present time but in the future. As the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) said just a few moments ago, in the revised statutes it is going to cause a certain amount of trouble and any further amendment to this act is certainly going to be a bit complicated.
Possibly the minister has a reason for this procedure; I do not know. It would appear to me, however, that if it is followed it is going to make it rather awkward for the members of the house, when the bill is

before us, to vote either for or against it, if there is anything in there that we do not like. Half of the amendments might be acceptable to us, or possibly all but one of the amendments might be acceptable to all of us; but we would have to vote against the bill and against what we might consider to be desirable amendments in order to attempt to defeat one clause or article in it.
It seems to me that it would have been much better all round if the minister had brought down these amendments in four separate pieces of legislation.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Beaudoin in the chair.

speakeroldname: Hon. Brooke Claxlon (Minister of National Defence):
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I do not think hon. members of the committee would want me at this stage to reply at length to the observations that have been made by the hon. members who have taken part in the discussion. However, I should like to say a word or two with regard to points that have been raised. First of all, with regard to the form of the bill, this is the third year in which a bill of this kind has been introduced. The National Defence Act was adopted in 1950 as an omnibus statute, for the first time since 1868 incorporating in one act all legislation with regard to defence, bringing it up to date and providing a uniform disciplinary code applicable to all three services. Naturally that legislation involved a good many consequential amendments to other statutes. By the time that act was put into effect I think there were some-the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre suggested a number, nineteen or something like that.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Seventeen or nineteen.

Seventeen or nineteen; I
think that is at least so. We in the Department of National Defence considered, with the Department of Justice, how this should be done. Nineteen or more different bills- each having six stages, as they have through this house, changing the word "thus" to "so" and the words "non permanent active militia" to "reserve forces" would take some time if put in separate bills. We also had in mind the fact that now we have considerable forces in Canada and it is desirable that the amendments be put in a form which can be incorporated into their books of military law promptly and effectively. So I took the advice of the Department of Justice and of the judge advocate general and thought that the best way to proceed was to have one bill as far as possible each year relating to defence matters right across the board, just as we did in the enactment of the National Defence Act itself. We had bills and statutes in 1950

and 1951. So far it has caused no inconvenience to anyone that has been brought to my attention, and has caused a great deal of convenience to the armed forces, which now have one statute each year to which they can look if there is any amendment that year. I think that is a pretty important point.
With regard to the observation of the hon. member for Nanaimo about the Geneva convention, we propose to adopt a law which will enable us to impose the sanctions to carry out our part of the conventions, irrespective of where an offence may occur, and to take action in the courts of Canada.
On our nationals.
Yes, that is right.
No other power will have the right to carry out punishment on our nationals.

I think that is right.
With regard to the final point relating to limitations on the salaries that may be obtained in the civil service by retired officers and men of the armed forces, as I said the last time that this resolution came before the house, this restriction does not apply to men; it applies only to officers. As it stands today the provisions of section 4, subsection 12 and section 52 of the Defence Services Pension Act, restrict an officer or warrant officer pensioner, appointed to the civil service, to that part of his pension which, when totalled with his salary, will not exceed the pay which he was in receipt of at the date of his retirement. The proposal here is to increase the ceiling so that he will get a salary and pension which combined will total his pay and allowances at the time of that date, not the date of his retirement.
The hon. member for Nanaimo has suggested that we should remove all limitations. That might be desirable from many points of view. Here I should like to pay a tribute to people like Rear Admiral Stephens who, after a long life of service in the navy, has worked for several years in a very senior and responsible position in the department, advising on labour relations. He himself rose from the lower decks and has done a most useful job for what must, after the deduction of income tax, amount to something like $2,500 a year over and above what he would have got from pension. That kind of case demands our full sympathy and consideration. But on the other hand Admiral Stephens, or someone in his capacity who retires at his seniority, if carried on in the department in a civilian capacity, would be entitled to something like the pay, position 55704-139
Canadian Forces Act
and responsibilities of an assistant deputy minister, let us say $10,000, $11,000, $12,000. His pension after 35 years' service and more was something like $6,000. With his pay and the pension of such an officer he would be getting $16,000 or more than the deputy minister or chiefs of staff. In other words, he would be profiting very substantially from his retirement, though continuing in the service of the same government department. That would not be a desirable thing. On that account it has not been the general policy of the government to treat civil service salaries and salaries received from private employers in the same way for the reason I have stated, and I do not see how else you could deal with it.
On the other hand, we think it is quite unfair that, in view of the increases in the pay and allowances of officers of the armed forces, he should not at least be entitled to draw from his combined pension and salary in the civil service up to what he would have been entitled to draw had he continued in the service and had advantage of the pay increase. So that, as the hon. member for Nanaimo said, this marks a step in the right direction, and I must say that the advisers of the government do not see how we can go any further in this direction without making it profitable for some officers to retire and take up positions in the civil service, if we are to enjoy their service.
What we want to do is to have officers serve as long as they can usefully serve in their service capacity. Then if they have qualities and capacities which are useful to the service of Canada in a civilian capacity, enable them to have a fair recompense for work which, while it may be inadequately paid for, is something they want to do.

I am not quite certain
whether I made my point clear or whether the minister did not quite get the essence of what I was trying to explain. I feel that while these amendments are good'-and I approve entirely of the assistance which is being given to the rear admiral, who is still employed'-I do not quite see the necessity of keeping a stricter limitation on the man who retires with a junior rank. The warrant officer has a stricter limitation placed upon his earnings, because at the date of his retirement, or at the present time, the pay of the rank of a warrant officer, of course, is not as high as the pay of the rank of an admiral. The pay of a captain is not as high as the pay of the rank of a colonel or a brigadier, and the limitation on the earnings in the civil service are based upon the pay of the rank at the present time. It is an improvement when it is based on the pay of the

Canadian Forces Act
rank on the date of retirement; but why should not the retiring warrant officer or the retiring captain, or whatever the junior rank may be, have the same opportunities of earning the same amount of money in the civil service without affecting his pension, as the more senior ranks? I was asking for an equitable limitation, not one which was based entirely upon rank. I do suggest that it could be overcome by perhaps putting on a ceiling, or something in the nature of a fixed amount, or perhaps by removing the limitation altogether. But under the present system we are perpetuating a disadvantage which has been in existence for years in respect of the more junior ranks. As I said, it affects the more junior ranks particularly, because the man who retires from those ranks has probably served' as a non-commissioned officer for most of his time, and only been recently promoted to, shall we say, a warrant officer or a captain, and has not had the opportunity of building up a reserve, which the officer retiring from the senior ranks would have.
I would ask the minister to give consideration to seeing whether it is not possible to find a way in which the limitation which will be imposed will be equitable on both the junior and the senior ranks.

I had not intended to speak on the resolution at all. If I were to do so it would be only with superficial knowledge. However I am struck with the form of the resolution, and I am seeking more information as to why it was presented in this form. Here we have lumped together half a dozen resolutions in what could be described as one omnibus piece of legislation. It is such a radical change from the usual form of resolution preceding a bill that I think we should be satisfied that it is a good form to follow before we proceed with it.
I listened to the brief explanation given by the minister, and I am not sure that I understood all of it. If I remember correctly the minister said that, after they are passed by the house, the amendments will be inserted in service books or records by the servicemen, and he thought that if they were in this form the servicemen could interpret the amendments readily. If I were a serviceman I would hesitate to try to untangle a bill with as many facets as this one appears to have.
I am wondering if there is not some other reason behind the form this has taken. The reason might be to avoid the necessity of bringing before the house five or six, or perhaps more, different resolutions preceding bills. That may be; and perhaps it would be a proper way to save time. But I want

to be sure that when we attempt to save time we do not get ourselves so confused that we will be like the centipede who, when he was asked how he knew what foot to put down first when he attempted to move, began thinking about it; and the more he thought about it the more he got tangled up, with the result that he could not move without falling down.
We may be reaching that point. I wish the minister would go a little deeper into his explanation of the form of the resolution. Thus far I am not satisfied.

I have little to add to what I said before. There have been many demands from various quarters to organize the business of the house. That is not my responsibility. But I think it is easy for members to see that if all the technical amendments relating to national defence can be brought forward at one time, then they can be dealt with at one time by the hon. members who are especially interested in defence. Also when we reach the committee stage the technical officers of the department-the judge advocate general, and other officers-can be here to give assistance. All of them would not have to wait to go through five or more different bills, either at the same or at different times.
It seems to me this procedure makes sense, from the point of view of the proper conduct of the business of the house; and it also makes sense from the point of view of the armed forces, because we have then each year one bill relative to the armed forces. It is tied into the loose leaf copy of the National Defence Act, without any difficulty at all.
Our experience in having this done this way in the previous two years, has not created the slightest difficulty.
In what form will these amendments to the bills be inserted in the loose leaf book?

They will be loose leaf
amendments cut off and tagged in.
Each portion will be tagged into its own particular act?
Yes.
But the acts in the loose leaf book are of course separate?
Yes.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I should like to ask a question which may be technical, but perhaps the minister can answer it. In the case of the rear admiral whose pension would have been $6,000, but who on going to work in the

minister's department ends up with a total emolument of $10,000, on what funds are those amounts drawn? Does he get the entire $10,000 from the funds of the department as civil service pay, or does he get $6,000 pension and $4,000 civil service pay?

I am subject to correction in the answer I make, because I have never had the question raised before. My view is however that he gets his pension from the defence services pension fund to which he has contributed. Then he would receive the balance of his pay from the department. However I should like to check on that before giving a final answer.

I should like to ask a question arising out of what was said a moment ago. Do I understand that when this bill passes it has the effect of amending the Defence Services Pension Act, the Civil Service Superannuation Act, the Royal Canadian Navy Act, and so on? When someone looks up one of these other acts, how does he have notice, unless he has an annotated copy? Are those amendments carried into the other acts, or do they rest solely in the measure we are now going to pass? In other words will amendments be made to the Defence Services Pension Act by this measure? How does one who picks up the Defence Services Pension Act know that this amendment has been made?

In the same way, and only in the same way, as he would know that an amendment has been made to any statute- either through reading the statutes passed each year, from the first chapter to the end, and making the necessary corrections, or by looking at an index. The index carries references to separate statutes.
That is not a complete answer because, as a matter of fact, in the case of most statutes, an office copy can be brought up to date, showing what has happened in each year.
Where there are consolidations bringing the acts up to date they carry the amendments.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Let us take the case of the Canadian Forces Act, 1951. I believe there was one in 1951. Will this bill affect our relations with United States forces stationed in Canada?
No.
I wondered whether it was the intention to amend any of those regulations.

No. We have an act relating to visiting forces which is applicable to the United States and which was enacted in 1947, if I recall correctly. Those statutes have been before the house several times and amended?
That is right.

The minister stated that the amendments to the National Defence Act will provide for penal sanctions and the bringing of offenders, regardless of their nationalities, before our courts. Supposing an American did commit one of the offences contemplated against the Geneva convention, if that were possible, would he be tried before a Canadian court or a United States court?

speakeroldname: Hon. George Prudham (Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
speechtext:
that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to extend the application of the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act to the years 1952 and 1953 and to clarify the provisions of subsection five of section three so as to provide for the assistance intended- when this subsection was enacted in 1951.
He said: Mr. Speaker, with your permission I should like to make a very short statement. I say a brief statement, because

Gold Mining
the matter of assistance to the gold mining industry was thoroughly discussed in this house less than a year ago, and I believe all hon. members are quite conversant with the subject.
On December 24 last my colleague, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott), announced that legislation would be sought at this session of parliament to continue the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act for a further period of two years, that is, for the calendar years 1952 and 1953.
It is well known that the gold mining industry has faced and is facing real difficulties as a result of rising costs and a fixed price for the industry's product. The government has been aware of this and for the past four years has met this situation by a cost-aid system under the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act.
In October 1951 gold producers were given access to premium markets for industrial gold. A number of mines took advantage of these arrangements and are continuing to do so. But this new outlet did not solve the problem of the higher cost mines. With costs continuing to rise, very serious consequences would face the industry should the cost-aid terminate at the end of 1951.
As I stated last year before this house, I hold that much of Canada's future growth is bound up in the development and colonization of our northern country, and gold mining is still the pioneer industry in opening northern Canada for development. It is therefore important that the life of these northern and western communities, the forerunners of our Canadian northward development, be safeguarded.
The bill which it is now proposed to introduce in this house is to provide for the extension of the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act to the calendar years 1952 and 1953 on the same basis as the 1951 formula. The bill will also clarify the application of
the formula for cost-aid in respect of the last quarter of 1950 and of the years 1951, 1952 and 1953.
The hope is hereby expressed that this extension of the act for two more years will encourage and assist the gold mines in meeting the continued high costs of production, and will be of benefit to those communities partly or wholly dependent upon them.

Mr. Speaker, there are a number of hon. members besides myself who wish to speak in a somewhat extended manner on this resolution. As the time still remaining would not permit me to complete my remarks this evening, I should like to move the adjournment of the debate.
